where χ0 is the intrinsic EVPA extrapolated to zero wavelength, assuming Faraday rotation in an external screen. For the depolarization measure, D > 0 corresponds to normal depolarization, in which the degree of linear polarization decreases toward longer wavelengths, whereas D < 0 indicates inverse depolarization, with polarization increasing toward longer wavelengths. The latter behavior may arise from complex emitting and Faraday-rotating structures (Sokoloff et al. 1998; Homan 2012; O’Sullivan et al. 2012). We discard D and RM measurements from low polarization states (LP < 0.5%), as well as measurements for which one or more SPWs deviate by more than 4σ from the best-fitting linear relation. The procedure for identifying outliers is described in Appendix D, and examples of the table products are shown in Appendix E.

3.3. Variability

The dataset analyzed here spans one to two weeks of observations per year over six years, providing the opportunity to study source variability on both weekly and yearly timescales. As Table B.1 shows, only a few sources were observed in more than five epochs, and most of these are in B6. Therefore, we focus the time variability analysis on B6 and for a selected subset of sources of interest: M87, Sgr A*, 3C273, 3C279, QSOB1921-293, NRAO530, 4C01.28, OJ287 and PKS1335-127.

We adopt a two-fold approach: (a) constructing time series of the measured parameters, and (b) evaluating their statistical distributions, computing averages, standard deviations, and variability indices. Details of these approaches are given in the following subsections.

3.3.1. Time series from ALMA measurements

To visualize the day-to-day and year-to-year evolution of the sources, we plot Stokes I, LP, EVPA, and RM measurements over time (Appendix F). This is shown for M87, Sgr A*, 3C273, and 3C279 in Figs. F.1, F.2, F.3, and F.4. To identify potential outliers and distinguish them from long-term trends, we compare our measurements to the ALMA Grid Survey (GS) light curves spanning 2016– 2026. The GS, conducted with the ALMA Compact Array (ACA), regularly monitors bright radio quasars in full-polarization mode alongside solar system calibrators. Data reduction uses the Analytic Matrix for ALMA PO- LArimetry (AMAPOLA3), providing near-uniform coverage of many targets at mm wavelengths since April 2012 (Kameno 2023). The GS dataset serves as an essential reference for assessing the calibration quality of our measurements. It overlaps with many VLBI targets, allowing us to place our observations into a broader temporal context. Only M87 and Sgr A* are not covered by the GS. The evolution of I, LP, and EVPA for the most frequently observed sources, binned into seven-day intervals, is shown in the figures of Appendix G.

Polarization maps provide important constraints for probing the magnetic field configuration in large-scale jets. We discuss the images of M87 (Fig. 2), Sgr A* (Fig. 3), 3C273 (Fig. 4), and 3C279 (Fig. 5) in Sect. 4, together with the observed trends in time and frequency of their core properties.

## 4. Results

In this section, we present the main results of the analyses described in Sect. 3. In Sect. 4.1, we summarize the spectropolarimetric behavior of selected well-sampled sources, considering both their temporal and spectral evolution. In Sect. 4.2, we explore systematic differences between object classes across the full sample.

4.1. Analysis of individual sources

Here we focus on a few individual sources: M87 (Sect. 4.1.1), Sgr A* (Sect. 4.1.2), 3C273 (Sect. 4.1.3), 3C279 (Sect. 4.1.4), NRAO530 (Sect. 4.1.5), QSOB1921-293 (Sect. 4.1.6), 4C01.28 (Sect. 4.1.7), OJ287 (Sect. 4.1.8), PKS1335- 127 (Sect. 4.1.9), and J1744-3116 (Sect. 4.1.10).

4.1.1. M87

In Fig. 2, we show Stokes I maps of the M87 radio galaxy at the three ALMA bands. The maps also include the corresponding LP fraction maps with EVPA orientation overlaid. The images reveal the kpc-scale jet of M87 extending from the core by ∼17′′ (1.4 kpc projected) at 343 GHz to ∼25′′ (2.1 kpc) at 93 GHz. The various jet knots are well resolved in the B6 image, while HST-1, located ∼0.9′′ (74.2 pc) from the core, is seen only in the high-resolution 343 GHz image (Goddi et al. 2025). The inner lobes are prominent at 93 GHz but are resolved out at higher frequencies. At cm and meter wavelengths, observations reveal much more extended, diffuse radio lobes, reaching scales approximately an order of magnitude larger (Owen et al. 2000).

From the LP maps, it is evident that the core is much less polarized (∼few %) than the jet (∼10 −60%); it is also less polarized than what is seen at horizon scales ∼10 −15% (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2021a,b), likely owing to the large amount of structure that is averaged inside the ALMA beam. The EVPAs are mostly perpendicular to the jet axis, except in knots A and HST-1, where they align with the jet, consistent with the presence of a large-scale helical magnetic field in the jet (e.g., Pasetto et al. 2021). For a helical field, this can be interpreted as the poloidal component dominating in regions with perpendicular EVPAs, while the toroidal component dominates where the EVPAs are parallel, possibly due to shocks compressing the field (Lyutikov et al. 2005). Alternatively, EVPA swings along the jet could be due to the kinematics of the different jet components, as relativistic aberration can cause components ejected at different angles to the line of sight to have distinct observed EVPAs. A more detailed study of the kpc-scale jet will be presented in a follow-up publication.

The evolution of Stokes I, LP, EVPA, and RM is reported in Table E.2 and plotted in Fig. F.1. The 1.3 mm flux density is relatively stable across years, with a median of 1.3 ± 0.1 Jy, it has the second lowest variability index for I, VI = 17.3%. The minimum flux was 1.08 Jy in 2018, and the maximum was 1.47 Jy in 2021. M87 displays significant spectral curvature in the wavelength range covered by VAPOLA (see upper panel of Fig. 1), going from slightly flat at 93 GHz to increasingly steeper at higher frequencies. The spectral index α also varies over time: it was around −1 at 221 GHz in 2017 and 2018, flattening to −0.65 in 2021, and steepening again to −0.9 in 2022.

M87 exhibits more variability in LP than in I, ranging from 1.0% to 2.8% (although it shows the lowest VLP = 51%). A slight decrease in LP at 221 GHz is observed over the years, from 2.5% in 2017 to 1.1% in 2022. The LP rises with frequency from ∼1.2% at 93 GHz to 2.8% at 343

The EVPAs at 221 GHz have a median of −0.4◦with a scatter of 4.4◦, excluding 2018 when they were ∼30◦. The frequency dependence of the EVPAs follows the expected λ2 relation within individual bands, but the magnitude of the RM tends to grow with frequency, and sometimes sign flips are observed across bands. For instance, in 2018, RM at 93 and 221 GHz was (6.0 ± 0.6) × 104 rad m−2 and (−4.3 ± 0.3) × 105 rad m−2, respectively. These variations may reflect different Faraday depths in the source or could be due to intrinsic variability, given the six day interval between observations in the two bands.

In fact, short-term RM variability on day-to-week timescales, often correlated with LP and EVPA changes, is ubiquitous at 221 GHz. In 2017 (Goddi et al. 2021), the RM in this band flipped sign over four days while LP rose from 2.1% to 2.7% and the EVPA shifted from −8◦ to −0.1◦. In 2018, the EVPA rotated by 12◦over three days while the RM magnitude decreased by ∼20% and LP remained stable at ∼2.2%. The opposite trend occurred in 2022: LP decreased from 1.33% to 0.94% while the EVPA remained stable and the RM magnitude increased over five days. 4.1.2. Sgr A*

Stokes I images of Sgr A* at ALMA bands B3, B6, and B7, corresponding to April 17, 2018, April 24, 2018, and April 15, 2023, respectively, are shown in Fig. 3. The extended minispiral is clearly visible at 93 GHz and 221 GHz but is largely resolved out at 343 GHz, with only its brightest patches above the noise. The diameter of the minispiral decreases from ∼40′′ (1.6 pc) at 93 GHz to ∼10′′ (0.8 pc) at 221 GHz, while the compact core is always detectable and brightens with frequency.

The averaged properties are reported in Table E.3 and plotted in Fig. F.2. Although Sgr A* is known to vary on timescales of minutes to hours (Baganoff et al. 2001; Genzel et al. 2003; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2022a,c; Wielgus et al. 2022), the day-averaged fluxes are among the most stable in the sample (VI = 16.9% and a median of 3.1 ± 0.3 Jy at 221 GHz). Peak and minimum fluxes are 3.7 Jy in 2021 and 2.6 Jy in 2017, respectively. Unlike most other objects in the sample, Sgr A* exhibits a flat or slightly rising mm spectral index, with a median and scatter at 221 GHz of α = 0.07 ± 0.15. The mm spectrum appears to peak between 200 and 340 GHz, consistent with broad-band (84 −720 GHz) observations by Liu et al. (2016). At ALMA scales, contamination from minispiral complicates the determination of the intrinsic Sgr A* spectrum (Albentosa-Ruiz et al. 2026). LP is moderately variable (VLP = 62.9%, with a median of 4.7 ± 1.6% at 221 GHz) and rises steeply with frequency, from < 1% at 93 GHz to 8.8% at 343 GHz in 2023. The highest LP was 7.1% in 2017, and the lowest was 1.7% in 2023. These values are much lower than the 24 −28% from horizon-scale images (Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2024). EVPA measurements show relative stability across years, with a median and scatter of −70.7±17.3◦, excluding 2018 and 2021. In 2018, the EVPA shifted from ∼−73◦on April 21-22 to ∼+70◦on April 24-25. Accounting for the nπ ambiguity, the change is more likely to have been ∼40◦, reaching ∼−110◦on April 24 (Albentosa-Ruiz et al. 2026). This transition coincided with a rise in LP from 3.8% to 4.4%, and a decrease in |RM| from (−6.3 ± 0.2) × 105 to (−1.6 ± 0.2) × 105 rad m−2 on April 22, before returning to (−4.6 ± 0.2) × 105 rad m−2 on April 24-25. A similar event occurred in 2021, when the EVPA went from +79◦ on April 14 to −89◦on April 17, passing through an intermediate state of −32◦on April 154. During this period, Sgr A* reached its highest flux density (3.7 Jy), LP increased from 4.7% to 5.7%, and |RM| dropped temporarily by an order of magnitude from (−5.7 ± 0.1) × 105 rad m−2 on April 14 to (−2.8 ± 1.1) × 104 rad m−2 on April 15, before returning to (−5.3 ± 0.1) × 105 rad m−2 on April 17. The depolarization reached its maximum during these jumps, (7.24 ± 0.24) × 10−4 GHz−1 on April 22, 2018, and (8.62 ± 0.23) × 10−4 GHz−1 on April 15, 2021, in a

4.1.3. 3C273

Images of the FSRQ 3C273 at ALMA bands B3, B6, and B7, corresponding to April 23, 2021, April 27, 2022, and April 19, 2021, respectively, are shown in Fig. 4. The jet extends up to ∼23′′ (87.5 kpc) from the core in the southwest direction, with a hotspot of peak brightness ∼200 mJy/beam about 1′′ upstream of the end of the jet. At 343 GHz, only the core and a faint jet of ∼0.5′′ (1.8 kpc) are visible; the extended emission is largely resolved out. The morphology is consistent with images at lower frequencies (Perley & Meisenheimer 2017; Harwood et al. 2022). Our maps show that the core is less polarized than the jet, which reaches ∼30% in B3 and ∼17% in B6. The EVPA in the core is generally counter-aligned with the jet (∼−50◦), while in the jet there are two distinct regions: an upstream section inheriting the core EVPA and a downstream section aligned with the jet. Such a change is consistent with shocks amplifying the toroidal magnetic field component.

Averaged quantities are reported in Table E.4 and plotted in Fig. F.3, . This is among the most variable sources in flux, with VI = 62.3% and a median of 4.7 ± 1.7 Jy. 3C273 showed roughly annual flares during 2017–2022 (Fig. G.1). Since 2022, it has remained in a relatively quiescent state. The spectral index at 221 GHz steepens over the years, from α = −0.68 in 2017 to −0.85 in 2021 and −0.9 in 2022. At 93 GHz, α was flatter: −0.34 in 2017 and −0.45 in 2018. Observations across three bands in 2021 show a consistent slope, α ∼−0.81±0.03, similar to B3 and B7 measurements in 2023 (α ∼−0.9). LP is variable (VLP = 73.4%), hovering around ∼2.3% during the oscillatory phase and rising to ∼5.1% in quiescence. Narrow-band observations frequently show inverse depolarization, with LP increasing toward longer wavelengths. For instance, in 2017, the LP decreased from 3.9% at 93 GHz to 2.4% at 221 GHz, with consistent depolarization measures of (−2.8±0.5)×10−4 and (−2.6±0.1)×10−4 GHz−1, respectively. Observations in 2022 (221 GHz) and 2023 (343 GHz) again show inverse depolarization in the range −[1.6, 0.4] × 10−4 GHz−1. While inverse depolarization was observed in several sources in this survey, 3C273 exhibits it most frequently. 3C273 is the source that most frequently shows inverse depolarization, which appears to be its natural polarization state during quiescence, as confirmed by AMAPOLA from 2022 onward.

EVPA measurements indicate core values of ∼−50◦in 2017, and ∼−32◦in 2018, 2022, and 2023. AMAPOLA data show a mean EVPA of −37.9◦with a scatter of 24.8◦. During the rising-flux week of April 2021, the EVPA appeared to flip from +76◦on April 13 and 15 to −85◦on April 18, while the 343 GHz measurement on April 19 was −64◦. 4.1.4. 3C279

In Fig. 5 we show images of the BLLac 3C279 from April 15, 2018, April 17, 2021, and April 15, 2023, at B3, B6, and B7, respectively. In the 93 GHz image, we see the southwest-pointing jet mostly blended with the core. There is also a less bright feature positioned about 13” (190 kpc) northwest of the core; this is a known structure that was already observed at cm wavelengths by de Pater & Perley (1983) and Cheung (2002), and it is visible in all of our 93 GHz maps, but not at higher frequencies, making it likely to be an old inflated radio lobe. We start to resolve a ∼5.4” (78.5 kpc) long jet at 221 GHz, and it is even better resolved at 343 GHz, where three distinct knots can be seen inside the first 2.2” (32.5 kpc) of extension, together with an extra, more distant one located about 4.4” (64 kpc) away from the core. The 343 GHz map of the jet is remarkably similar to Figure 2 of de Pater & Perley (1983) at 5 GHz. Our maps do not show much of the polarized extended emission due to the low signal of the jet, but they do illustrate how the core’s EVPA can change on yearly timescales, as it is oriented along the jet axis in some years and against it in others.

Measurements are reported in Table E.5 and plotted in Fig. F.4. The 221 GHz flux oscillated around 7.4 ± 2.8 Jy before 2021, peaked at ∼13 Jy during 2021–2022, and has since declined to ∼3 Jy, making 3C279 the second most variable source in flux (VI = 61.5%). The spectrum of this BLLac is also nicely characterized by a power law that changes slightly depending on the year. The spectral index is well described by a power law that steepens slightly with frequency (α ∼−0.4 at 93 GHz versus ∼−0.6 at 221 GHz), flattens during flaring (α = −0.5 in 2021), and steepens in quiescence (α = −0.9 in 2023). 3C279 was observed in the three ALMA bands during the flare of 2021 and in 2023. The LP of 3C279 fluctuated significantly during the 2016–2026 interval, with VLP = 87.8%. Our measurements show a median and scatter of (10.1±2.7)% at 221 GHz, but the wider coverage of AMAPOLA shows (7.3 ± 3.4)%. LP also shows a long-term decline from ∼15% in 2017 to ∼6% in 2022, followed by a partial recovery to ∼10% at the end of the flaring state in 2023; it has remained below 5% since the end of 2024. There is a clear increase in LP across bands in both 2021 and 2023, with the LP going from ∼6% at 93

GHz to ∼10% at 343 GHz, accompanied by a decrease in depolarization toward higher bands. From 2017 to 2020, the EVPAs of 3C279 remained consistently around 40◦. This changed at some point between 2020 and 2021 (during a gap in monitoring due to the COVID-19 pandemic coinciding with the onset of the flaring state), when it reached around −60◦and then drifted to ∼17◦in 2023. Given the nπ ambiguity, an equivalent scenario involves a +80◦rotation to ∼120◦in 2021; either way, both scenarios involve changes close to 90◦. We discuss a possible scenario that could be responsible for this change in Sect. 5.1. The EVPAs have been unconstrained since late 2024 due to the very low polarization. The RM of this BLLac is low (≲few×104 rad m−2 at 93 and 221 GHz) and is frequently undetected, but it increases substantially with frequency, reaching (−1.2 ± 0.3) × 105 rad m−2 at 343 GHz in 2021. The RM can also change sign depending on the year.

4.1.5. NRAO530

The averaged properties of NRAO530 are reported in Table E.6. ALMA measurements indicate that the 221 GHz flux density was 1.7 ± 0.1 Jy in 2017–2018, decreasing to ∼1.4 Jy in 2021 and further to 0.86 Jy in 2022. The AMAP- OLA light curve supports this trend and shows more erratic variability between 2016 and 2019, followed by a more quiescent phase from late 2021 onward (VI = 58.1%). The spectral index at 221 GHz (α ∼−0.9 ± 0.1) remains fairly stable over the years, and is slightly steeper than the values measured at 93 GHz (α = −0.59). According to AMAPOLA, this source is among the most LP-variable in the sample (VLP = 96%, range 0–7.7%), and its frequency behavior changed between campaigns: normal depolarization (LP increasing from 93 to 221 GHz) was detected in 2017, giving way to inverse depolarization in 2018. The LP peaked at 7.7% in 2021, with normal depolarization again detected at 221 GHz. EVPA and RM are poorly constrained in most epochs due to the generally low LP, with EVPAs oscillating around (15 ± 20)◦from 2021 onward and negative RMs in the range ∼104–105 rad m−2 where detectable. At sub-pc scales, EHT imaging resolves polarized emission in multiple components of the inner jet of NRAO530 (Jorstad et al. 2023); differently oriented components would blend together within the ALMA beam and could help explain why the EVPA and RM are so poorly constrained here.

4.1.6. QSOB1921–293

Quasar QSOB1921–293 (J1924–2914) is used as a routine calibrator for Sgr A*. ALMA measurements at 221 GHz show that this FSRQ was largely stable (3.2±0.7 Jy) during 2017–2021 before entering a flaring state (5.7±0.5 Jy) from late 2021 through late 2023; its flux variability is comparable to that of 3C273 and 3C279, with VI = 60.7%. The spectral index varies with epoch, becoming flatter (α ∼−0.6) during the 2021–2023 flare, and generally steepens with frequency. The evolution of averaged quantities is shown in Table E.7. QSOB1921–293 is strongly variable in linear polarization, with VLP = 90.5%. Both our measurements and AMAPOLA show LP values of (5 ± 2)% during 2017–2020,

There is evidence for inverse depolarization during the 2018 observing week, when D reached (−1.4 ± 0.2) × 10−4 GHz−1 at 221 GHz on April 22. The EVPAs of QSOB1921–293 are predominantly negative. They ranged between −50◦and −40◦in 2017–2018, became unconstrained on several days during the lowpolarization phase associated with the rising flux in 2021– 2022, and settled around −30◦in 2023. At VLBI (subpc) scales, the inner jet is very polarized (up to 25%) and has a predominantly toroidal magnetic field (Issaoun et al. 2022). Significant RM detections are rare for this source, with the two most robust measurements being of opposite sign: (7.3 ± 1.4) × 104 rad m−2 at 221 GHz in 2018 and (−9.2 ± 1.3) × 104 rad m−2 in 2023. For the non-detections at 221 GHz, the values fluctuate around zero prior to 2021, shift to moderately positive values (∼4 × 104 rad m−2) in 2021, and become mildly negative in 2023 (∼−3 × 104 rad m−2).

4.1.7. 4C01.28

Our measurements of quasar 4C01.28 are reported in Table E.9. The 1.3 mm flux density is typically around 2.8±0.5 Jy. This BLLac object is among the least variable sources in our sample, with a variability index of VI = 49.9% derived from the AMAPOLA data. A modest flaring episode occurred between late 2018 and early 2019, after which the source settled into a stable state at ∼2.5 Jy. The spectral index was seen to steepen with frequency (α from −0.47 at 93 GHz to −0.9 at 221 GHz) in 2017 and 2018. In contrast, the spectrum was flatter in 2021, with α ≃−0.6 at 93 GHz and α ≃−0.4 at 343 GHz. LP is strongly variable (VLP = 96.7%), dropping from ∼5.5% in 2017 to a minimum of 0.9% in 2018. Consistent with this, the frequency behavior of LP transitioned from normal depolarization in 2017 (LP rising from 93 to 221 GHz) to inverse depolarization in 2018 during the low- LP state. The EVPAs at 221 GHz are also highly variable, showing significant swings and multiple apparent flips over the 2017–2025 period. It changed from −23◦to −14.4◦over six days in 2017. In 2018, a rapid change of nearly 40◦(from −28◦to +12◦) was observed over four days, while the RM changed sign from positive to negative, coinciding with an increase in LP by a factor of 1.5. In 2021, EVPAs were consistently ∼−38◦across 93 and 343 GHz with a small RM of (−7.9 ± 0.7) × 103 rad m−2 at 93 GHz, and a non detection at 343 GHz around ±3.5 × 104 rad m−2.

4.1.8. OJ287

The averaged properties of OJ287 are reported in Table E.10. This quasar is moderately variable in flux at 221 GHz (VI = 43.7%, median 3.2±0.8 Jy), but shows many small oscillations in the AMAPOLA light curve. The spectral index is also variable at 221 GHz(α ∼−[1.1, 0.7]) and appears to steepen with frequency (α ∼−0.6 at 93 GHz). The LP of OJ287 is more variable than its total flux, with VLP = 74.9% and typical values of (9.0 ± 2.8)%. For

example, the LP decreased from ∼9% on April 5, 2017 to ∼7% on April 10–11. The highest LP at 221 GHz, 12.8%, was measured on April 27, 2018, coinciding with a period of unusually low flux density (1.85 Jy). OJ287 generally shows weak but normal depolarization, both within individual bands and across bands. However, during this highpolarization, low-flux state we detected significant inverse depolarization, with D = (−2.1 ± 0.2) × 10−4 GHz−1 at 221 GHz. OJ287 is the only BLLac in our ALMA sample that exhibits inverse depolarization. The EVPA measured at 221 GHz was approximately −62◦in 2017, increased to −34◦in 2018, and was −46◦ in 2022. The broader AMAPOLA dataset yields a median EVPA of (−36 ± 18)◦over the 2017–2025 period. The frequency dependence of the EVPA generally results in relatively small RMs (≲104 rad m−2 at 93 GHz), but it changed sign at 221 GHz between 2017 (positive) and 2022 (negative). The first EHT imaging of OJ287 identified three components in the inner jet with significant EVPA evolution across five days (Gómez et al. 2026), which suggests that part of the variability seen by ALMA originates at VLBI scales.

Our measurements are reported in Table E.11, and they show that the 221 GHz flux density of PKS1335–127 varies substantially from year to year. ## 5. Discussion

In this section, we summarize the variability trends and discuss physical scenarios that could account for the observed changes (Sect. 5.1), and examine the RM versus frequency behavior and investigate whether it can provide insights into jet geometry (Sect. 5.2).

5.1. Short and long-term time evolution

For sources observed multiple times within the same week, we generally do not detect significant changes in total intensity or spectral shape on daily to weekly timescales. Instead, substantial variations in flux density and spectral index predominantly occur over yearly timescales. With the broader temporal coverage provided by AMAPOLA, we interpret the ALMA measurements as snapshots capturing the sources at different stages between low- and highactivity states. Spectral evolution is most evident in sources that experienced flaring episodes. These events are typically characterized by a spectral flattening during the flare, followed by a steepening in subsequent years. For instance, both 3C279 and QSOB1921–293 exhibited relatively flat spectra during their flares, with α ∼−0.53 and α ∼−0.57, respectively5. In contrast, 3C273 showed an unusually steep spectrum during its 2021 flare, with a consistent α = −0.8 across all three bands. In all cases, a spectral steepening is observed after the flare, which can be attributed either to synchrotron cooling or to the fading of the flaring component (Marscher & Gear 1985; Türler et al. 2000). On short (weekly) timescales, polarization properties exhibit substantially stronger variability than total intensity or spectral index. The LP can vary by factors of 0.5 to 2 from one day to the next, often accompanied by abrupt changes in EVPA and RM. In several sources, increases in LP appear to correlate with decreases in |RM|, and vice versa. This is observed in M87 (2017, 2022) and Sgr A*

5 The spectrum of QSOB1921–293 was already flatter in 2021, prior to the flare peak observed in 2022.

(2018, 2021). Conversely, other quasars, such as 3C273 during its 2021 flare, 4C01.28 in 2018 and PKS1335–127 in 2022, show either opposite trends or no clear correlation between LP and RM on short timescales. For sources such as 3C279, QSOB1921–293, and OJ287, polarization variability on weekly timescales is comparatively modest. However, these objects typically exhibit weak RM signals that can drop below detectability from one day to the next, and their RM can change sign across different years. This behavior is also observed in M87 and 3C273 in the ALMA data and was previously reported for 3C273 and 3C279 using VLBA observations by Zavala & Taylor (2001).

On long timescales, the most pronounced polarization changes tend to coincide with flaring activity. In particular, large EVPA rotations are observed in 3C273 during its 2021 flare and in 3C279 between 2020 and its major flare in 2021. One plausible interpretation is that these variations are associated with the emergence or evolution of unresolved jet components, as suggested by Anderson et al. (2019). Such behavior is expected in shock-in-jet models developed to explain polarization variability in VLBI cores at centimeter wavelengths (Blandford & Königl 1979; Lind & Blandford 1985; Marscher & Gear 1985; Hughes et al. 1989a; Qian et al. 2002). The ejection of new components with polarization properties distinct from those of the core could naturally explain the simultaneous increase in flux, as well as changes in polarization and RM observed in these sources. Contemporaneous VLBI polarization imaging could be used to test this scenario by constraining the spatial scales at which the variability originates. Arrays such as the GMVA (∼ 60 µas) and the EHT (∼ 20 µas) probe sub-pc scales in 3C273 and 3C279, while the VLBA, EVN, and KVN (∼ 0.7 mas) are sensitive to structures on parsec scales (Lister et al. 2018; Okino et al. 2022; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2025). In the case of Sgr A*, the daily polarization variability appears decoupled from the long-term evolution of flux and spectral index, although the limited statistics should be noted. A long-standing tension exists between the consistently negative RM measured for Sgr A* (Bower et al. 2018; Wielgus et al. 2024) and horizon-scale GRMHD simulations, which predict highly variable RMs that frequently change sign on hourly timescales (Ricarte et al. 2020; Ressler et al. 2023; Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration et al. 2024). However, the polarization light curves presented in (Albentosa-Ruiz et al. 2026) covering the 2018 EHT campaign show that the RM of SgrA* can vary significantly and even take on positive values for short periods, with a characteristic variability timescale of ∼30 minutes. If confirmed, this would constitute strong evidence towards internal Faraday rotation within the accretion flow itself. Given these considerations, we expect the intraday RM curve from April 15 2021 should be marked by strong and/or frequent sign flips in hourly timescales to explain the very low |RM| we measure from the time-averaged data (see Sect. 4.1.2); this will be explored in a forthcoming publication. In an attempt to cross-compare the variability features specific to different classes, we can use the variability study conducted in Sect. 3.3.2. 5.2. Frequency dependence of the RM

The Faraday RM is sensitive to both the density of the magnetized medium traversed by the radiation and to the magnetic field component along the line of sight, following equation:

RM = 8.1 × 105 Z neB∥· dl rad m−2, (7)

where ne is the electron number density (cm−3), B∥is the magnetic field component parallel to the line of sight (G), and l is the path length through the plasma (pc).

Since synchrotron opacity decreases with increasing frequency (Blandford & Königl 1979; Konigl 1981), observations at different bands are expected to probe physically distinct regions of the source. In particular, higher frequencies should originate closer to the central engine, where both the electron density and magnetic field strength are presumably higher. Under a set of simplifying assumptions, Jorstad et al. (2007) showed that the RM magnitude should scale with observing frequency as a power law, |RM| ∝νa. The main assumptions are: (1) the plasma density decreases with distance from the central engine as ne ∝r−a, with a = 2 for a conical or spherical outflow and a < 2 for more collimated flows; (2) the toroidal magnetic field dominates the line-of-sight component, B∥∼Bϕ ∝r−1 (Begelman et al. 1984), as expected if the Faraday screen is even mildly relativistic; (3) the effective integration length is proportional to the distance, l ∝r; and (4) the core-shift effect (discovered by Marcaide & Shapiro 1984), whereby the distance between the VLBI core and the central engine decreases with increasing frequency due to the medium becoming more optically thin, with r ∝ν−1 as expected under equipartition (Lobanov 1998; O’Sullivan & Gabuzda 2009a). Combining these assumptions leads directly to a power-law dependence of the core RM on frequency, |RM| ∝νa. Using VLBI RM measurements at 8, 15, and 43 GHz, Jorstad et al. (2007) estimated a for several sources, including 3C279 (a = 0.92), 3C345 (a = 1.6), and 3C454.3 (a = 1.8). Later, Hovatta et al. (2019) analyzed 3C273 over a much broader frequency range (4.7–220 GHz) and obtained a = 2.0 ± 0.2. Other studies have reported values spanning a ∈[0.9, 4] (O’Sullivan & Gabuzda 2009b; Kravchenko et al. 2017; Kam et al. 2025).

Given our multi-band ALMA coverage, we investigated the dependence of the rest-frame RM magnitude, |RM|rest, on the rest-frame frequency νrest = (1 + z)ν for the bestcovered sources in our sample, and explored the implications for their jet geometry. We included all tentative RM measurements with SNR> 2 and performed simple powerlaw fits to derive a global index aall for each source. Since most sources were observed in only one band per year, we combined data from all epochs, but we also performed yearby-year fits when multi-band observations were available in order to minimize the effects of intrinsic variability and to assess temporal changes in a. This analysis was carried out for nine well-sampled sources, shown in Figure 9, with results summarized in Table 3. PKS1335–127 was excluded due to the lack of reliable RM measurements. The power-law indices obtained from the mm/sub-mm ALMA observations lie in the range of a ∼[0.7, 4.4], consistent with values from the literature at lower frequencies but covering a slightly wider range. The values for M87 are consistent throughout the years aall ≃2.37 ± 0.34. Sgr A* had an apparently lower index in 2023 (0.66) than in 2017 (1.06), but both are roughly consistent with the value obtained from fitting all years aall = 1.23 ± 0.22. The index of 3C273 seems to have been much higher in 2017 (∼4) than in 2021 or 2023. Whether the decreasing index observed in 3C279 reflects genuine structural changes remains unclear, particularly in light of its major flare in 2021 and the transition to a more quiescent state in 2023. Within this framework, the larger

indices found for 4C01.28, OJ287, and J1744–3116 may indicate more rapidly expanding flows, while the lower values measured for NRAO530 and Sgr A* would be consistent with more collimated outflows. We find no clear association between a and source class, as both FSRQs and BL Lacs span the full range of measured indices.

The case of Sgr A* is particularly intriguing. Although a jet has not yet been conclusively confirmed in this source, multiple lines of indirect evidence point to its existence, including large-scale non-thermal radio structures aligned with the Galactic rotation axis (Yusef-Zadeh et al. 1986; Sofue et al. 1989), spectral energy

Our RM– frequency analysis could therefore provide an additional indirect indication of a highly collimated outflow in Sgr A*, assuming the Faraday rotation originates in such a structure. Alternatively, the accretion flow itself could act as the Faraday screen. This is argued by the works of Marrone et al. (2006); Li et al. (2015); Bower et al. (2018) and is also supported by GRMHD simulations (Ricarte et al. 2020; Ressler et al. 2023). If we revisit assumption (2) about the magnetic field configuration, and follow Marrone et al. (2006) in adopting a radial magnetic field profile tied to the electron density in the form B∥∝r−1

2 (a+1), then the expected behavior of the RM will also follow a power law |RM| ∝νa′, with a′ = 1 2( 3

2a + 1). This yields a more restricted range a′ ∈[0.875, 1.625], corresponding to convectiondominated and spherical/advection-dominated flows, respectively (Blandford & Begelman 1999; Narayan & Yi 1994; Quataert & Gruzinov 2000; Marrone et al. 2006; Park et al. 2019). This illustrates that a power-law RM dependence on frequency may not be a unique feature of jet-dominated Faraday rotation.

Another important caveat is that the framework of Jorstad et al. (2007) assumes that the polarized emission observed from the VLBI core at a given frequency ν originates predominantly from a single τν ∼1 region in the jet. In practice, however, the core itself may contain unresolved substructure and, particularly for sources viewed close to the line of sight, the observed polarization represents the integration of emission from multiple regions along the jet. Moreover, spatial variations in the magnetic field and electron density of the Faraday screen, as well as spectral evolution of the synchrotron emission, may modify the relative contributions of these regions to the observed polarization. The combined effect of these components on the observed |RM| ∝νa relation is not yet well understood, as multiple Faraday screens can produce non-linear EVPA–λ2 behavior (Sokoloff et al. 1998; O’Sullivan et al. 2012). This issue is particularly relevant for ALMA observations, whose arcsecond-scale resolution blends emission that can be spatially resolved by VLBI experiments. Nevertheless, we find no clear dependence of the index a on source class. Quantifying the impact of unresolved Faraday components and frequency-dependent polarized emission on the observed RM–frequency relation is beyond the scope of this work and will be investigated using the multi-band polarization data presented here in a forthcoming publication.

## 6. Conclusions

We have presented a spectropolarimetric study of a sample of AGN and Sgr A* observed with ALMA during GMVA and EHT VLBI campaigns between 2017 and 2023. The observations span several days over one to two weeks per year and cover three ALMA bands, enabling a characterization of the spectral and polarization properties of compact cores over the 86–345 GHz (0.87–3.4 mm) range. The full sample

consists of 39 targets, including 29 quasars (22 FSRQs, 7 BL Lacs, 1 unknown), 9 active galaxies, and Sgr A*. We analyzed in detail the subset of best-sampled sources and investigated their temporal and spectral evolution over the full observing period. Our main results can be summarized as follows:

– On weekly timescales, most sources show limited variability in total intensity and spectral index (VI < 10%), while larger changes are commonly observed from year to year. – Polarization properties often vary on much shorter timescales, with abrupt changes in polarization fractions and EVPA occurring from one day to the next. When considering the full 2017–2023 dataset, typical variability indices are VI ∼60% and VLP ∼80%. – Large EVPA rotations observed during flaring states may be linked to the evolution of unresolved jet components. This interpretation can be tested through direct comparison with contemporaneous and future VLBI imaging observations. – BLLac objects are systematically more polarized than FSRQs at mm and sub-mm wavelengths. Active galaxies show significantly lower polarization fractions than quasars and SgrÃ*, with the latter reaching LP values of up to ∼9% at 343 GHz, comparable to those measured in BLLacs. – For most sources, the polarization fraction increases with observing frequency. FSRQs account for nearly all counterexamples, displaying as many episodes of inverse depolarization as regular depolarization. In particular, 3C273 exhibits inverse depolarization even during quiescent states, suggesting the presence of persistent and complex Faraday structures that require detailed modeling over a broad wavelength range. – The large RMs observed (∼104–105 rad m−2) point to ordered magnetic field structures close to the central engine. These RMs are generally stable within a given observing week but can change sign from one year to the next. – In a few cases, rapid RM sign reversals or strong decreases in magnitude are observed over timescales of days, coinciding with episodes of rapid polarization variability, indicating a dynamically evolving Faraday screen. – Using the multi-band ALMA coverage, we find evidence for a power-law dependence of |RM| on frequency, with indices in the range a ∼0.7–4.4. These values are consistent with Faraday rotation originating in a magnetized sheath surrounding the relativistic jet, allowing constraints to be placed on jet geometry. An origin in the accretion flow remains a viable alternative, particularly for Sgr A*, for which a collimated jet has not been firmly established.

Appendix C: Uncertainty budget

The uncertainties in the Stokes parameters include statistical errors from the visibility-domain fitting with UVMUL- TIFIT (Sect. 3.1) and systematic calibration contributions. For Stokes Q and U; we adopt the systematic leakage of 0.03% of Stokes I, while for Stokes V we adopt 0.6% of Stokes I. These values correspond to one third of the ALMA minimum detectable linear (0.1%) and circular (1.8%) polarization levels quoted at the 3σ level for compact sources (see ALMA Technical Handbook6). The statistical and systematic contributions are added in quadrature. The uncertainty in ALMA’s absolute flux calibration, estimated at 5% in Band 3 and 10% in Bands 6 and 7, affects all Stokes parameters as a common multiplicative factor. We therefore do not include this contribution in the uncertainties of individual SPW measurements, since it is correlated across the simultaneously observed SPWs and Stokes parameters. Treating it as an independent error would artificially inflate the uncertainties in the derived spectral and polarization quantities, particularly the spectral index α, LP, and EVPA. We include the absolute flux calibration uncertainty in the band-averaged Stokes I measurements and image-based flux densities, for which the absolute flux scale is relevant. The uncertainties in LP and EVPA are obtained by propagating those of the Stokes parameters, including the adopted systematic polarization calibration terms. For the band-averaged LP and EVPA, we additionally include the standard deviation across the four SPWs to account for their observed frequency-dependent scatter. The uncertainties in fitted quantities such as α, D, and RM are derived from the corresponding fits, using the individual SPW uncertainties. The statistical analysis and quality-control procedures are described in Appendix D.

For nested models satisfying the regularity conditions of Wilks’ theorem, TS approximately follows a χ2 distribution with k = k1 −k2 degrees of freedom, where k1 and k2 are the numbers of free parameters in the two models. This allows us to estimate the statistical significance of the improvement in the fit. In this work, we consider linear relations, m(x) = ax+b, including power-law relations fitted in logarithmic space. Their significance is evaluated relative to a constant null model, mnull(x) = c, which represents the absence of a dependence between the two quantities.

D.1. Outlier rejection

For quantities derived from fits across the four SPWs, such as D and RM, we apply an additional quality-control procedure to identify measurements potentially affected by anomalous SPWs. For fits with a significance below 2σ, we perform a leaveone-out test. Each SPW is excluded in turn, and a linear relation is fitted to the remaining three measurements. We then compare the excluded measurement with the value predicted by this relation. We reject the corresponding D or RM determination if at least one SPW deviates from the prediction by more than four times its quoted measurement uncertainty. This procedure resulted in the rejection of 30 measurements among D and RM, corresponding to approximately 7% of the total.

D.2. Reliability of in-band RM measurements

The uncertainties used in the RM fits include both thermal noise and the systematic polarization calibration terms described in Appendix C, propagated to the EVPA measurements of each SPW. After applying the quality-control procedure, most retained RM measurements are consistent with a linear EVPA–λ2 relation within their quoted uncertainties, with a median reduced χ2 of 0.3. The mean EVPA uncertainty is σχ ≃0.25◦per SPW across all bands, comparable to values reported in previous ALMA polarization studies (e.g., Nagai et al. 2016; Hull et al. 2020; Goddi et al. 2021). # Polarimetry of Black Hole Spin and Axisymmetric Emission Geometry

**Authors:** Vadim Bernshteyn Affiliation: Steward Observatory and Department of Astronomy, University of Arizona, 933 N. Cherry Avenue, Tucson, AZ 85721, USA Daniel C. M. Palumbo Affiliation: Center for Astrophysics $|$ Harvard & Smithsonian, 60 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Black Hole Initiative at Harvard University, 20 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Dominic Chang Affiliation: Center for Astrophysics $|$ Harvard & Smithsonian, 60 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Black Hole Initiative at Harvard University, 20 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Tintin Nguyen Affiliation: Center for Astrophysics $|$ Harvard & Smithsonian, 60 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Affiliation: Black Hole Initiative at Harvard University, 20 Garden Street, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA

## Abstract

The Event Horizon Telescope array has measured the average polarimetric spiral morphology of black hole accretion disks using the so-called “ $\beta_{2}$ ” coefficient. This measurement is dominated by the weakly lensed, direct ( $n=0$ , counting photon half-orbits) image of the disk, providing insight into magnetic field structure around the M87* black hole. The future space-based Black Hole Explorer mission is expected to extend these capabilities, allowing for $\beta_{2}$ measurement of the strongly lensed $n=1$ image. In this paper, we explore the constraints $\beta_{2}$ measurements would impose on spacetime and plasma geometries using a semi-analytic conical emission model. We show that magnetic field orientation with respect to the emission cone qualitatively changes the dependence of $\beta_{2}$ modes on model parameters. For cone-aligned magnetic fields, we find that the leading-order theoretical prediction from equatorial emitters of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}\approx\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*}$ is the dominant trend even in off-equatorial models. Specifically, we show $\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\,\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*})\approx 4\chi$ , where $\chi$ is the angle determining in-cone magnetic field orientation. We also find that $\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\beta_{2,\,n=1})$ minimizes the effect of magnetic field geometry while preserving a dependence on spin that may be used to measure spin direction. We find that observations of the photon ring’s $\beta_{2}$ complement the constraint from direct image polarization, and can greatly constrain magnetic field structure even with an unknown external rotation measure. We also find that black hole spin and emission cone opening angle would not be tightly constrained by $\beta_{2}$ alone, unless strong priors are placed on the magnetic field geometry.

## I Introduction

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) collaboration has made horizon-scale images of supermassive black holes commonplace by linking the world with a global sub-mm very-long-baseline interferometry (VLBI) array. Though the first images of Messier 87* (hereafter M87*) were a triumph of engineering and data science, combining interferometric visibilities in the Fourier domain to reconstruct the on-sky image, the downstream theoretical interpretation and black hole parameter estimate remained limited by our understanding of black hole accretion and its relationship to the lensed image [12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17].

From the very first treatments of these black hole images, the hunt for measurements of mass and spin has been dominated by morphological signatures in the image, as distant viewers see a “shadow” with size and shape specified by these parameters along with the viewing inclination [1, 37, 23, 31]. The mass-to-distance ratio of the black hole scales the angular size of lensed features such as the “inner shadow” (the direct image of the horizon) and the “photon ring” (the sharp ring feature formed from multiply-lensed copies of the accretion disk), whereas spin and inclination warp these features from circles to more asymmetric shapes [27, 33, 3, see, e.g.]. While these features are shaped more by the spacetime than by the astrophysics of the surrounding accretion disk, they are subtle, and not yet well-constrained by existing Event Horizon Telescope images of the near-horizon plasma [15, 20, see, e.g.].

Indeed, EHT theoretical constraints more often produce indirect measurements of properties such as the mass, spin, accretion rate, and disk magnetization through comparisons of low-resolution image properties to those extracted from models, such as semi-analytic radiatively inefficient accretion flows (RIAFs) or general relativistic magnetohydrodynamical (GRMHD) simulations [16, 17, see, e.g.]. One such image property that is prevalent in images of gently inclined accretion disks is the polarization spiral pattern, expressed using the so-called $\beta_{2}$ parameter [42]. This parameter expresses the overall pitch angle of a spiral pattern in polarization using the phase of a complex coefficient, related directly to the axisymmetric magnetic field through the polarization of synchrotron radiation.

Image polarization, through analyses of $\beta_{2}$ , has been identified with trends in spin in two general forms. First, studies of GRMHD simulations in Palumbo et al. [42], and later in semi-analytic treatments of Blandford-Znajek monopolar and parabolic solutions as well as RIAFs, have shown that the large-scale magnetic field structure carries spin information far beyond the ergosphere. Regularity conditions at the horizon ultimately emerge as a trend in the electric vector position angle (EVPA) at larger radii that rotates by nearly $90^{\circ}$ as spin varies from minimal to maximal [2, 4, 29, 55]. These analyses apply for equilibrium, axisymmetric field conditions obeying a family of magnetospheric assumptions which may not hold in the full generality of accretion systems found in nature.

Second, irrespective of the underlying magnetic field, a fixed polarized emitter necessarily encodes spin information as the polarization vector is transported to a distant observer .This effect was first treated for X-ray polarization in Connors et al. [8], and studied for highly lensed near-horizon emission by Himwich et al. [28] and Gelles et al. [25]. A previous analysis in Palumbo [44] treated spin inference from optically thin synchrotron emission from the Kerr midplane. One may treat the problem of spin inference in polarization while allowing for more flexibility in the emission geometry. In this paper, we extend the analysis of Palumbo [44] to emission off the equatorial plane, and provide a more robust treatment of the broad polarimetric phenomenology of the first two lensed sub-images of the accretion disk.

To do so, we manually set an emitting profile for a source using an analytic model from [5] which showed that most GRMHD simulations can be well approximated by a combination of 3 two-dimensional emitting surfaces: the equatorial plane of the accretion disk, and two conic surfaces representing the front and back components of the jet. We target just the lensed polarization properties of one surface, which we modulate in polar angle. By restricting to a single cone, we maximally isolate the geometric contributions from the different magnitudes of lensing experienced by the first two sub-images traversing distinct polar sweeps on the way to the observer, as well as geometric effects from the location of the emitter and the parameters of the spacetime itself.

We begin with a review of the cone model and its appearance in polarization in Section II. We then study the dependence of the direct and indirect image $\beta_{2}$ quantities in a survey of models with different emission and magnetic field geometries in Section III. We then consider sums and differences of the direct and indirect image $\beta_{2}$ quantities as a means of removing the contribution from the unknown magnetic field geometry or the unknown rotation measure (respectively) in Section IV. We present our conclusions in Section V.

## II Synchrotron Emission from a Cone in Kerr

Here we give a brief review of the conical emission models from [5]. The authors defined multiple models for the time-averaged appearance of M87*, with the full best-fit model consisting of 3 conic surfaces. The model extends previous semi-analytic models for optically thin emission in the midplane (Narayan et al. [39] treated Schwarzschild, while Gelles et al. [25] and Palumbo et al. [40] extended the model to Kerr). This model provides an analytic approximation for the time-averaged structure of emission around a black hole, and it matches particularly well with GRMHD models of the M87* black hole. Since in this paper we focus on a phenomenological study of polarization patterns and symmetries arising from lensing in Kerr, we will only consider models consisting of a single conic surface for simplicity. We will refer to these models as single-cone emission models hereafter. 11 1 While the total Stokes $I$ intensity images of the conical models were analyzed in detail in [5], the same models can also be used to produce Stokes $Q$ and $U$ linear polarization images.

### II.1 Model Setup

The single-cone emission model comprises both parameters pertaining to the plasma flow and parameters pertaining to the spacetime geometry, and as such is a powerful tool for studying one group of parameters assuming the other group is relatively well-constrained (for a full description of parameters at play see Table 1). In particular, because the emission model parametrizes the plasma relative to the zero angular momentum observer (ZAMO) frame, it is naturally suited to “all else equal” studies of the impact of black hole spin. In this paper, we mostly focus on inferring spacetime parameters once there is a sufficiently good guess for the magnetic field orientation. Of course, the precise and complete constraining power of the model based on observed data requires one to consider both plasma and spacetime parameters together in one high-dimensional optimization problem. In Section IV, we propose two new observables which roughly separate polarization imprints due to spacetime and due to magnetic field configuration, but otherwise we defer performing the full optimization on real data to future studies. More broadly, the model itself contains no treatment of spatially or temporally varying (turbulent) plasma properties, and the constraints we study from measurements of polarimetric image quantities contain no notion of an instrument model, let alone a full analysis pipeline. Thus, we only aim to demonstrate some simple dependencies in the model to gain some intuition about polarization from off-equatorial accretion features, such as the jet base.

We use the Krang software package for numerical ray-tracing of the emission models [6]. It is important to mention some limitations of the package. Throughout the paper, a “face-on” observer corresponds to a viewing inclination angle set to $\theta_{o}=1\degree$ , as the ray-tracing is not numerically reliable when the angle is set precisely to $\theta_{o}=0\degree$ . Similarly, a “non-spinning” black hole corresponds to a numerical model of a black hole with $a_{*}=0.01$ . For our purposes these differences are negligible. A schematic of the single-cone model setup and examples of resulting $n=0$ Stokes I images are shown in the top two rows of Figure 1. The package uses Bardeen $\alpha$ and $\beta$ coordinates on observer’s screen, which are dimensionless quantities measured in $\frac{GM}{c^{2}d}$ , where $M$ is the mass of the black hole and $d$ is the distance to the black hole from the observer.

*Figure 1: Illustration of single-cone models for different cone opening angles $\theta_{s}$ . Top row shows schematic of emission geometry around a black hole for each $\theta_{s}$ . Rows 2-4 show Stokes I, Q, and U images of $n=0$ and $n=1$ rings for each model, as would be seen by a face-on observer. Colors represent pixel brightness scaled to the highest value in each individual subplot. The imaging was done assuming the following single-cone model parameters: $a_{*}=0.9$ , $\chi=-90\degree$ , $\eta=90\degree$ , $\iota=90\degree$ , $\beta_{v}=0.5$ , $R=4$ , $p_{1}=p_{2}=4$ .*

Emission from M87* observed by EHT is believed to be produced primarily by synchrotron radiation [57, see, e.g.]. As such, it is expected to be linearly polarized perpendicularly to the underlying magnetic field when observed at frequencies at which the emitting material is optically thin, and at a resolution for which beam depolarization is negligible. Turbulent sub-structure in the magnetic field can reduce the degree of polarization, a major contributor to differences in polarization morphology among fluid models [42]. Since the Event Horizon Telescope is expected to greatly improve its polarization sensitivity and resolution with future next generation Event Horizon Telescope [10, ngEHT,] and Black Hole Explorer [32, BHEX,] projects, it is interesting to study what insights into the spacetime and emission geometry polarization images provide.

Examples of $Q$ and $U$ signatures of the single-cone models for different cone geometries are shown in the bottom two rows of Figure 1. It is clear that the resulting polarization patterns change significantly as the geometry of the emission changes. We also observe that polarization patterns depend on the black hole spin in a manner fundamentally different from the total intensity images, as the orientation of polarization carries additional information about the frame dragging experienced by the emitting plasma. While we generally defer a full 3-surface treatment to future work, we show the analogous breakdown for the complete midplane-and-dual-cone model in Appendix A.

The central polarization quantity we investigate in this paper is the $\beta_{2}$ mode, first introduced in Palumbo et al. [42]. $\beta_{2}$ is a complex number quantifying rotational symmetry in the observed polarization pattern. Specifically, $|\beta_{2}|$ quantifies the degree of rotational symmetry in the $P=Q+iU$ image, and $\arg(\beta_{2})$ represents the overall pitch angle of the polarization pattern, as each coefficient encodes an integrated projection of the image against simple azimuthal basis functions. In this work, we consider only the fully radially integrated $\beta_{2}$ coefficient:

$$ \displaystyle\beta_{2} \displaystyle=\dfrac{1}{I_{\rm tot}}\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi}P(\rho,\varphi)\,e^{-i2\varphi}\;\rho\mathop{\mathrm{d}\varphi}\mathop{\mathrm{d}\rho}, $$

where $I_{\rm tot}\equiv\iint_{\rm image}I\,\mathop{\mathrm{d}x}\mathop{\mathrm{d}y}$ is the total Stokes $I$ flux density in the image, and $\rho$ and $\varphi$ define radial and azimuthal image coordinates.

$\beta_{2}$ has been measured from polarimetric observations with the EHT since the first imaging of M87* and Sgr A*, and used in downstream theoretical analyses as an image-domain model comparison metric, especially for comparisons to GRMHD [21, 22, 18, 19, 50]. The coefficient also permits a Fourier analogue described in Palumbo et al. [41]; as the spiraling polarization handedness is expected to swap between the direct and indirect image [28, 43], so too does the Fourier analogue flip in sign as the indirect image dominates long baselines. Moreover, the direct and indirect image $\beta_{2}$ may be independently estimated even with limited Fourier coverage that is otherwise insufficient for imaging [48, 49]. The future BHEX space mission [32] is expected to probe the M87* image on scales where the signal from the $n=1$ photon ring would dominate the $\beta_{2}$ signal, thus providing us with two separate $\beta_{2}$ measurements for $n=0$ and $n=1$ . As we demonstrate below, $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ show different dependencies on model parameters, meaning measuring both simultaneously would have greater model-constraining power.

### II.2 Basic Dependencies of $\beta_{2}$

*Figure 2: $\arg(\beta_{2})$ in degrees as a function of black hole spin $a_{*}$ and cone opening angle $\theta_{s}$ . Left panel is constructed for $n=0$ rings only, and the right panel is for $n=1$ rings only. The underlying plasma model is: $\chi=-90\degree,\eta=90\degree,\iota=90\degree,\beta_{v}=0.5,R=4,p_{1}=p_{2}=4$ . Imaging was done at observer inclination $\theta_{o}=17\degree$ .*

We start by considering $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ dependence on dimensionless black hole spin $a_{*}$ and cone opening angle $\theta_{s}$ for a single plasma model. We choose the following parameters for our model: $\theta_{o}=17\degree,\chi=-90\degree,\eta=90\degree,\iota=90\degree,\beta_{v}=0.5,R=4,p_{1}=p_{2}=4$ . We choose these parameters to approximate the appearance of M87*, for which we assume the spin inclination to match that of the jet observed at large scales [54, 34]. With these parameters fixed, we vary black hole spin $a_{*}$ and cone opening angle $\theta_{s}$ in the ranges $a_{*}\in[-1,1]$ , $\theta_{s}\in[60\degree,120\degree]$ . Then, for each combination of $a_{*}$ and $\theta_{s}$ , we rendered $n=0$ and $n=1$ images of the full model using Krang, and computed $\beta_{2}$ for each image. Finally, we produced heatmaps of $\arg(\beta_{2})$ as a function of $a_{*}$ and $\theta_{s}$ .

The results are shown in Figure 2. We see that phases of both $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ change significantly with $\theta_{s}$ and $a_{*}$ , which demonstrates that $\beta_{2}$ modes indeed encode spacetime information. It is especially promising to see that $n=0$ and $n=1$ modes show different patterns in their geometry dependence, such that measuring $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ will yield qualitatively new information that is, at least partially, independent of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ .

*Figure 3: $-\arg({\kappa^{2}})$ in degrees for each light ray on screen. Images are generated for $n=0$ rings of $\theta_{s}=90\degree$ cones around black holes with spins $a_{*}=-0.9$ , $0$ , and $0.9$ . All other model parameters are the same as in Figure 2. The black region satisfies the condition that the flux-per-pixel is at least 200 times smaller the maximum flux-per-pixel in the image $I_{\text{black}}<\frac{1}{200}\max(I_{\text{image}})$ , and is manually masked out.*

The precise analytic dependence of the observed $\beta_{2}$ mode on the black hole spin $a_{*}$ is sensitive to the geometry of the emitting material, as well as the embedded magnetic field. To better understand the geometric dependencies within the observed polarization, we may turn to the Penrose-Walker constant $\kappa$ , a complex number that is conserved along null geodesics in the Kerr spacetime [53]. Polarization ray-tracing in Krang is done by computing Penrose-Walker constants at each point of emission, and then using these constants to derive polarization of light rays on the observer’s screen. The constant mixes dependencies from black hole parameters, the location and magnetization of the emitter, as well as the location of the observer (in setting the direction of the emission of light):

$$ \kappa=(A-iB)(r-ia_{*}\cos\theta), $$

where

$$ \begin{split}A&=k^{t}f^{r}-k^{r}f^{t}+a_{*}\sin^{2}\theta(k^{r}f^{\phi}-k^{\phi}f^{r}),\\
B&=\left[(r^{2}+a_{*}^{2})(k^{\phi}f^{\theta}-k^{\theta}f^{\phi})-a_{*}(k^{t}f^{\theta}-k^{\theta}f^{t})\right]\sin\theta,\end{split} $$

$k^{\mu}=(k^{t},k^{r},k^{\theta},k^{\phi})$ is the null geodesic 4-vector, $f^{\mu}=(f^{t},f^{r},f^{\theta},f^{\phi})$ is the polarization 4-vector, and $(t,r,\theta,\phi)$ are Boyer-Lindquist coordinates at the point of emission. While the presence of several distinct orders of spin dependence in $\kappa$ means we ought to expect spin information in downstream polarimetric observations, the particular connection to $\beta_{2}$ is not obvious by inspection. In an upcoming paper (Nguyen et al., in prep.), it is shown that for modest spins $a_{*}$ and observer inclinations $\theta_{o}$ , the $\beta_{2}$ mode can be well-approximated by an intensity-weighted integral over the image-plane value of $\kappa^{2}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\beta_{2} \displaystyle\approx\frac{m}{I_{\rm tot}}\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\int\limits_{0}^{2\pi}I(\rho,\varphi)\left(\frac{{\kappa}^{*}(\rho,\varphi)}{|\kappa(\rho,\varphi)|}\right)^{2}\;\rho\mathop{\mathrm{d}\varphi}\mathop{\mathrm{d}\rho} $$

provided that the linear polarization fraction $m$ is constant across the image; essentially, the argument of $\kappa$ manifests straightforwardly as EVPA, albeit defined with opposite handedness because of the complex conjugation of $\kappa$ in Equation 4. Our single-cone emission models prescribe a narrow emission profile and a constant polarization fraction ( $m=1$ ), the appropriate regime to use Equation 4 to relate $\arg(\kappa^{2})$ with $\arg(\beta_{2})$ . We caution that the latter simplifying assumption is rather unrealistic as more physically-motivated GRMHD simulations have shown that the linear polarization fraction could vary substantially on the image due to turbulence in the accretion flow and optical/Faraday depth effects [22, 46, see, e.g.]. Nevertheless, our study focuses on the phase of $\beta_{2}$ , which is not affected by the constant polarization fraction prescription. The nature of the connection between $\beta_{2}$ and black hole spin implicitly expressed through $\kappa$ in Equation 4 can be seen in Figure 3. Here we compute $-\arg(\kappa^{2})$ for each light ray hitting the screen, assuming we know the spin and inclination of each model exactly (this information is needed for $\kappa$ calculation). We do so for models with $a_{*}=-0.9$ , $0$ , and $0.9$ . For simplicity, we assume a cone opening angle of $\theta_{s}=90\degree$ (equatorial plane), and all other model parameters are the same as in Figure 2. We see that changing spin tends to rotate $\kappa^{2}$ for each light ray. While the exact amount of rotation is different for different light rays and different plasma models, the average rotation of $\kappa^{2}$ on the screen corresponds almost exactly to the rotation of the $\beta_{2}$ mode. As a result, Equation 4 provides insight into how the $\beta_{2}$ mode, which is purely a property of an image, is connected to the spacetime parameter $a_{*}$ .
