First, note that we do not perform a fully complete sampling of the parameter space, nor is our survey dense enough for inference, meaning the relative densities in $\beta_{2}$ distributions we obtain should not be taken as precise. That being said, we consider a vast and fairly unconstrained space of models, so we still expect major resulting trends to describe behavior typical for polarized emission in the absence of Faraday effects.

Second, we fix the observer’s inclination angle $\theta_{o}$ at $17\degree$ to mimic the measured inclination of M87*; though the inferred inclination on jet scales obtained by Walker et al. [54] and Kim et al. [34] carry order-degree uncertainties, the much larger relevant uncertainty is systematic, in the case where M87*’s spin axis is gently tilted with respect to the jet, a mismatch caused by a possible disk tilt [9, 7, supported by some evidence of wobble, see, e.g.]. However, as studied in Qiu et al. [45], the phase of $\beta_{2}$ is nearly invariant with viewing angle between inclinations of 0 and $\sim 30^{\circ}$ , far beyond the reasonable range expected for M87*; thus, we expect inclination uncertainties to be largely irrelevant to the emergent phenomenology of this work.

We restrict $\eta$ to always equal $\chi+180\degree$ , as magnetic flux freezing causes magnetic field to point roughly in the direction opposite to the fluid flow by the time the fluid reaches the near-horizon region [see, e.g. 47, for visualizations of the near-horizon magnetic field structure]. While we survey the value of $\iota$ , the angle made by the magnetic field with the emission cone, we generally expect $\iota$ to remain close to $90^{\circ}$ , especially for emission surfaces above or below the midplane (that is, corresponding to coronal or jet funnel structures). This expectation follows from general tendencies for plasma motion in these highly magnetized regions, in which particle motion is largely restricted to flow parallel to field lines. These dynamical properties were studied in detail in GRMHD with accompanying field line tracers in both Mościbrodzka et al. [38] and Wong et al. [56], which together suggest that both in the near-horizon region and at larger distances in the jet, the entrained magnetic field appears mostly parallel to the primary emitting surfaces. We also restrict individual radial contributions: we fix $p_{1}=p_{2}=10$ , which corresponds to a very narrow emission profile on the cone, where most of the emission is coming from a circle at distance $r=R\frac{GM}{c^{2}}$ from the black hole. We choose narrow emission bands in order to avoid smearing of radially dependent effects within a single emission profile.

In the main body of this work we focus on the phase of the $\beta_{2}$ mode, as this value is expected to be most accurately predicted by the single-cone model when compared to real black hole observations, especially those at high frequency with low corresponding Faraday rotation depths. $\arg(\beta_{2})$ has also been shown to correlate with the black hole spin in GRMHD simulations [4, 11, 45, 55]. By contrast, the amplitude of the mode $|\beta_{2}|$ is not expected to be predicted accurately by the single-cone model due to the assumed (unrealistic) polarization fraction of $m=1$ and the absence of both Faraday rotation and small-scale turbulence, which causes depolarization at finite resolution. Despite this deficiency, comparison of $|\beta_{2}|$ between different single-cone models might still provide insight into how geometric effects alone affect the observed polarization fraction at finite resolution. We find that the angle $\iota$ the magnetic field lines make with the surface of the cone significantly changes the overall polarization of both the direct image and the photon ring. We put a more detailed discussion of $|\beta_{2}|$ trends in Appendix B.

### III.1 Overall Distribution

The resulting distribution of $\beta_{2}$ modes across our models is shown in Figure 4. The plot shows $\log_{10}$ of the number of models falling into each bin, where the bins represent specific values of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ measured in the image. The size of each bin is $4\degree$ both in $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and in $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ .

We see that most models tend to fall on the main diagonal of the heatmap, which corresponds to $\beta_{2,\,n=0}\approx\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*}$ . The equality is expected to be exact for pairs of $n$ , $n+1$ images for large $n$ from equatorial emission in Schwarzschild [28]. Models that are strongly offset from the diagonal tend to be produced by exotic orientations of the magnetic field, as can be seen in the $\iota=45\degree$ and $\iota=0\degree$ subplots. Overall, low and high values of $\iota$ seem to show qualitatively different patterns, making it difficult to characterize trends in $\beta_{2}$ without any $\iota$ constraints. Since we expect real black holes to have magnetic field lines approximately tangent to the surface of a jet, we will mostly focus on the $\iota=90\degree$ case in our analysis.

We see that $\iota=90\degree$ models closely follow the $\beta_{2,\,n=0}\approx\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*}$ relation. A closer look at the dataset shows that the high clustering of models on a few evenly spaced points on the diagonal is due to sparse sampling in $\chi$ , with each cluster corresponding to a specific $\chi$ value imaged. More generally, a detailed analysis of the dataset suggests that $\iota=90\degree$ models follow two trends in $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ - $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ space: a location on the main diagonal is primarily determined by the magnetic field orientation $\chi$ , and the off-diagonal variation is primarily determined by spacetime parameters $a_{*}$ and $\theta_{s}$ . This observation suggests a natural change of coordinates, where one coordinate measures the location on the diagonal and the other measures off-diagonal deviation. We explore this new set of coordinates in Section IV.

### III.2 Parameter-Specific Trends

*Figure 5: $(R,\,\arg(\beta_{2}))$ plots in polar coordinates for models with different $\theta_{s}$ and spin. In each plot, radial coordinate is $R$ , and angular coordinate is $\arg(\beta_{2})$ . All models shown have $\theta_{o}=17\degree$ , $\beta_{v}=0.5$ , $\chi=-135\degree$ , $\eta=45\degree$ , $\iota=90\degree$ . Spin is represented by color, with $n=0$ and $n=1$ measurements using different color scales. The offset in $R$ between $n=0$ and $n=1$ values is set artificially for visual clarity.*

Let us now consider specific trends in parameter space in greater detail. First, we fix $\theta_{o}=17\degree$ , $\chi=-135\degree$ , $\eta=45\degree$ , $\iota=90\degree$ , and $\beta_{v}=0.5$ . Then we vary $\theta_{s}$ among the set $[60\degree,75\degree,90\degree,105\degree,120\degree]$ . This way, for each $\theta_{s}$ , the only variables left to be free in our parameter space are emission radius $R$ , black hole spin $a_{*}$ , and the ring number $n\in\{0,1\}$ . We depict all of these parameters in Figure 5 in the following way: $R$ is treated as the radial coordinate in a polar-coordinate plot, and $\arg(\beta_{2})$ is treated as the phase coordinate. To represent spin, we use color, and we use different color palettes for $n=0$ and $n=1$ .

We see that for $n=0$ rings, larger $\theta_{s}$ corresponds to larger variance of $\beta_{2}$ with spin. This makes intuitive sense, as light from a forward jet undergoes a weaker gravitational lensing effect before reaching the observer compared to a backward jet. It also seems that, when averaged over spin, values of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ are largely independent of the value of $R$ . This suggests that the observed $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ trends would mostly remain the same when wider emission profiles (smaller values of $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ from Table 1) are considered.

For $n=1$ rings, changing $\theta_{s}$ seems to have almost no spin-averaged effect on the dependence of $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ on $R$ . This suggests that $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ might be used to constrain the $R$ parameter of the model. Variance of $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ with spin also seems to depend on $R$ : for small $R$ , the variance tends to decrease as $\theta_{s}$ moves from forward to backward jet, whereas for large $R$ the variance tends to increase.

The trends identified above seem to hold for most models in the parameter space. If this is the case, our results suggest that model fits to data of the single-cone model (or spiritually similar approaches) will constrain spin holistically according to this approximate “procedure”: First, $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ gives an initial idea about the structure of the magnetic field (constraining $\chi$ and $\iota$ ). Then, the values of $\chi$ and $\iota$ can be used together with $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ to constrain $R$ , since $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ appears nearly independent of $\theta_{s}$ . Knowing $R$ from both total intensity imaging and $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ , we can constrain $\theta_{s}$ by considering the magnitude of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ rotation at a given $R$ . Remaining variation in $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ then constrains the spin. In reality, these constraints all occur simultaneously in the Bayesian forward modeling employed by the single-cone model.

However, the very first step in this causal chain depends on knowing the phase of $\beta_{2}$ , which is only possible if the external rotation measure is well-measured. Moreover, the knowledge of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ appears to primarily pin a point along a fundamental diagonal in the space of observed spiral phases, indicating that parameterizing spin dependence orthogonal to the diagonal will reduce complexity without losing access to the most interesting physics. Thus, we now turn to phase sums and differences of $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ .

## IV $\Delta$ - $\Sigma$ space

*Figure 6: Distributions of $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ in models with $\iota=90^{\circ}$ and $-180\degree\leqslant\chi\leqslant-90\degree$ . Top: Marginal distribution of $\Delta$ against $\chi$ , $a_{*}$ , and $\theta_{s}$ . Bottom: Marginal distribution of $\Sigma$ against the same parameters.*

We define

$$ \begin{split}\Delta&\coloneqq\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*})=\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0})-\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=1})\\
\Sigma&\coloneqq\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\beta_{2,\,n=1})=\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0})+\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=1})\end{split} $$

as a basis for a new coordinate system in $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ - $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ space. These new coordinates are orthogonal in the apparent parameter space identified in Figure 4 and as such encode mostly independent information about the model. Specifically, $\Delta$ measures the location along the main diagonal in Figure 4, while $\Sigma$ measures the distance from the diagonal ( $\Sigma=0$ corresponds exactly to the main diagonal).

Distributions of $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ with respect to magnetic field orientation, spin, and cone opening angle are shown in Figure 6. We restrict our analysis to models with $\iota=90\degree$ , as these are the models where the benefits of the new coordinate system are most apparent. We examine the deviation from the trends identified in this section later in Appendix C. For conciseness and visual clarity, we also assume infalling clockwise-rotating flow ( $-180\degree\leqslant\chi\leqslant-90\degree$ ) with respect to the spin axis, even though the trends we discuss are not specific to this range of $\chi$ . From the plot we see that $\Delta$ appears to have a strong dependence on the magnetic field orientation, while providing little insight into spacetime parameters $a_{*}$ and $\theta_{s}$ . On the contrary, $\Sigma$ appears to have a significant correlation with spin, while seemingly having no correlation with $\chi$ . This agrees with the intuition that $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ , being orthogonal coordinates quantifying two distinct trends in $\beta_{2}$ space, should separate magnetic field and spacetime effects as cleanly as possible. We discuss specific trends and observational prospects of each of the coordinates below.

### IV.1 $\Delta$ Quantity

$\Delta$ is a coordinate that follows closely the magnetic field orientation in the model, as can be seen in Figure 6 (Top Left panel). In particular, we find that

$$ \Delta\approx 4\chi $$

to within $\sim 20\degree$ variation in $\Delta$ caused by spacetime effects. It is clear that $\Delta$ is a good predictor of $\chi$ (up to $90\degree$ rotation), and as such it might be an interesting observable for the BHEX mission.

Future observations of $\Delta$ might be especially useful due to its independence of the external rotation measure. Using traditional $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ to constrain the spin of M87* is complicated by the need to assess the magnitude of a rotation measure (RM) in order to accurately measure $\beta_{2}$ modes [see, e.g. 26, and its impact on the model scoring in the downstream polarimetric analyses from the 2017 data]. Rotation measure quantifies the extra rotation of polarization pattern induced by the medium along the line of sight. Since $\arg(\beta_{2,\,\text{observed}})\approx\arg(\beta_{2,\,\text{source}})+2\text{RM}\lambda^{2}$ (with $\lambda$ the observing wavelength, see Kulsrud [35]), the accuracy of measuring both $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ relies heavily on the accuracy of RM measurement. Previously, it has been shown that in the current EHT setup RM is not tightly constrained [50, see, e.g.], which in turn might weaken constraints obtained from $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ . We note that any remaining difference in the total internal Faraday rotation between $n=0$ and $n=1$ would still be present in $\Delta$ , while the external rotation (beyond the near-horizon region) is fully removed by construction. As studied in Jiménez-Rosales et al. [30], the $n=1$ ring can appear depolarized in 230 GHz images of simulations of the M87* accretion flow, even when the $n=0$ image is polarized, largely attributable to the increased Faraday rotation depth of the more highly winding rays. However, as described in greater detail in Palumbo and Wong [43], in models in which the photon ring is polarized at all, the polarization is generally coherent and exhibits a conjugation structure similar to the one found in this study.

### IV.2 $\Sigma$ Quantity

$\Sigma$ is, on the other hand, a coordinate that shows correlation with the black hole spin $a_{*}$ , while being relatively independent of the magnetic field orientation (Figure 6, Bottom Left and Bottom Middle). To be precise, the Pearson correlation coefficient between data points shown in the bottom middle panel of Figure 6 is $p\sim-0.6$ , indicating a statistically significant linear dependence between $\Sigma$ and $a_{*}$ . The least-squares fit of this linear dependence gives

$$ a_{*}\approx-0.02(\Sigma/\deg) $$

where $\Sigma$ is restricted to $[-50\degree,50\degree]$ and is measured in degrees. If the relation were exact, it would imply that a $\pm 1\degree$ measurement of $\Sigma$ would constrain the black hole spin $a_{*}$ to $\pm 0.02$ precision. Put another way, the slope of $\Sigma$ is $\sim 50^{\circ}$ per unit spin. Matching the typical spin imprint magnitude with instrument sensitivity to obtain a spin measurement of $\pm 0.1$ precision requires a measurement of the indirect image polarization phase to better than $\sim 5^{\circ}$ , corresponding to a signal-to-noise ratio of $\sim 11.5$ in polarimetric visibilities, which is stringent but likely achievable on the most sensitive BHEX baselines [32]. It bears emphasizing that sensitive polarimetry is generally challenging in VLBI, with stringent needs for high polarimetric purity and parallactic angle coverage in order to successfully calibrate leakage terms [21, see, e.g.]. While the orientations of the $n=0$ and $n=1$ EVPA are generally widely separated in angle for non-radially-infalling flows (and thus more tolerant of small systematic deviations in polarimetric orientation calibration in differential measurements), full degeneracies between gain ratios and linear polarization such as those that emerge in purely linear-feed VLBI could in principle completely destroy the expected signal [51]. Thankfully, virtually all proposed sub-mm interferometric expansions currently under consideration either use all-circular feeds (shifting this degeneracy from linear to circular polarization), or have mixed polarimetric feeds.

Unfortunately, without stronger assumptions on the magnetosphere, the spread of the fit in Equation 7 is quite high, as is visually apparent from the gentleness of the slope in the bottom middle panel of Figure 6 compared to the apparent spread of the model set. In our dataset the standard deviation from this fit is $\sim 0.47$ units of spin, as shown in Appendix C. This means that in the absence of additional model constraints a measurement of $\Sigma$ would only roughly constrain the overall direction (into or out of the page) of the M87* spin vector, which is so far only constrained by brightness asymmetry in GRMHD library comparisons [16, see, e.g.]. In addition, unlike $\Delta$ , $\Sigma$ is not a relative quantity and as such depends on the external RM measurement. In the absence of other constraints on the geometry of the emitting material (such as those inferred from image morphology, which is neglected in our analysis), even a highly sensitive polarimetric measurement on BHEX baselines would be dominated by this intrinsic variation among models.

## V Conclusions

In this paper, we studied polarimetric $\beta_{2}$ modes of a semi-analytic single-cone model, focusing on the dependence on cone opening angle, black hole spin, and magnetic field orientation. We did so by sampling the parameter space of the model and ray-tracing corresponding emission cones. The study was done separately for $n=0$ and $n=1$ rings, as the future BHEX and ngEHT missions are expected to probe M87* on scales where $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ modes are separable. We proposed $\Delta=\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*})$ as a quantity that is independent of external rotation measure and that can be used effectively to constrain magnetic field orientation $\chi$ in future observations. We also proposed another quantity, $\Sigma=\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0}\beta_{2,\,n=1})$ , as a potential tracer of black hole spin. Provided that $\iota$ remains within a few tens of degrees of $90\degree$ , these two quantities obey simple trends with respect to both magnetic field orientation and spin.

In general, we find that the relationship between $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ and spin is sensitively dependent on the geometric parameters describing the emission location and magnetic field. For cases where magnetic field lines are constrained to the surface of the cone ( $\iota=90\degree$ ), magnetic field orientation is the primary parameter determining $\beta_{2}$ for both $n=0$ and $n=1$ . The dominant trend is: $\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=0})=\arg(\beta_{2,\,n=1}^{*})=2\chi-180\degree$ . Deviations from this trend do not exceed $\sim 20\degree$ , and are caused by spin and geometric effects. As magnetic field lines move out of the cone’s surface, the dependence of $\beta_{2}$ on magnetic field orientation weakens, and for $\iota=0\degree$ $\beta_{2,\,n=0}$ and $\beta_{2,\,n=1}$ are primarily determined by spin and cone geometry.

Our analysis permits a large volume of potentially unphysical magnetic field geometries in our model survey when constructing spin distributions; this model space stands in contrast to magnetospheric solutions constructed to match expected conditions in a magnetized accretion disk around a realistic black hole [2, 4, 29, 55, see, e.g.], for which much stronger, order-unity deviations in polarization orientation are expected from black hole spin. More generally, our model makes no connection between the black hole spin and the astrophysical parameters of the model, whereas more realistic disk-jet systems likely carry spin information in the geometry of their emission. In this way, our model may be viewed as pessimistic in its total access to spin information, though it is also optimistic in its simplicity, particularly in its reduction of the emitting region to a single cone.

It bears emphasizing that the single-cone model studied in this paper leaves out sub-structural details of real accretion disks and their lensed images that will ultimately set a floor in systematic uncertainty of future spacetime measurement efforts. Ideally, models fit to multi-frequency measurements of accretion flows could self-consistently capture the full four-dimensional structure of the plasma as well as the frequency-dependent radiative transfer through the disk and jet in parallel with the spacetime model, resolving turbulence through high-resolution, high-cadence observations. While such models would carry heavy computational expense, they are already under development, and have been applied with heavy assumptions under which the problem is well-posed even with currently available data (such as a midplanar emission geometry with a vertical field, explored in Levis et al. [36] and Feng et al. [24]). As such models grow in complexity, their interpretability and pedagogical value decline; thus, we turn to simple models such as the single-cone model treated here to better understand the source of spin information in potential future measurements. Studies that connect these maximally general accretion disk prescriptions to full forward models of an interferometric array [52, e.g.] are already underway, and their resulting spin measurement projections will be more decipherable in light of forerunner studies such as ours.

Ultimately, our analysis provides estimates of the magnitude of a spin imprint in polarization which must be present in time-averaged observations of the first two lensed images at sufficiently high frequency to be optically- and Faraday-thin, while remaining agnostic to many possibly-stronger signatures which depend on astrophysics we leave unspecified. In this way, we provide a fundamental floor on instrumental capabilities for missions targeting these lensed structures.

## Appendix B $|\beta_{2}|$ Trends

*Figure 8: Distribution of models from Figure 4 in $|\beta_{2,\,n=0}|$ - $|\beta_{2,\,n=1}|$ space. Size of an individual bin is $0.01\times 0.01$ .*

In the main body of the paper we focused on the phase angle $\arg(\beta_{2})$ of the $\beta_{2}$ modes found in our models. While the magnitude $|\beta_{2}|$ can be computed using the same numerical procedure, this quantity is expected to carry less physical significance. This is due to the polarization fraction of $m=1$ assumed in the single-cone model, which is expected to be unrealistic for plasma emitters around real black holes. As a result, the polarization magnitude predicted in our models is unrealistically high. Moreover, the absence of Faraday rotation effects in Krang ray-tracing calculations increases this disparity even more. However, even though the absolute values of $|\beta_{2}|$ are physically meaningless, the relative coefficient magnitudes across our surveyed parameter grid can still provide insight into the intrinsic effects of emission geometry on the rotational symmetry of the polarization field. As such, we provide $|\beta_{2}|$ distributions we obtained here.

Analogous to Figure 4, the distribution of all models considered in this study in $|\beta_{2,\,n=0}|$ - $|\beta_{2,\,n=1}|$ space is shown in Figure 8. We see that lower angles of $\iota$ tend to produce weaker $\beta_{2}$ signatures both in the direct image and in the photon ring. We observe that, even for a totally axisymmetric magnetic field geometry viewed at a small inclination, the degree of rotational symmetry in the observed polarization can degrade by tens of percent solely by virtue of more poloidal magnetic field orientations, rather than a lack of symmetric magnetic field conditions. This result echoes the vertical field diagrams in Narayan et al. [39] and Gelles et al. [25], in which modest inclinations cause purely vertical fields to look dramatically asymmetric.

## Appendix C Sensitivity to $\iota$

*Figure 9: Comparison of $\Delta=4\chi$ and $a_{*}=-(0.02/\degree)\Sigma$ fits to models with different magnetic field inclination angles $\iota$ . The top row shows the distribution of values $\Delta-4\chi$ for different $\iota$ . The bottom row shows the distribution of values $a_{*}+(0.02/\degree)\Sigma$ . The dashed lines show the standard deviation $\sigma$ in each case. Note that, unlike in Figure 6, there is no $\chi<-90\degree$ restriction, so the plots show distributions across all available models.*

Our main analysis finds simple relationships $\Delta=4\chi$ and $a_{*}=-0.02(\Sigma/\deg)$ for models where $\iota=90\degree$ . We may study the impact of more exotic magnetic field line inclination angles by examining the distributions of the deviation from these trends as $\iota$ varies from $90\degree$ . In Figure 9, we plot the distributions of $\Delta-4\chi$ and $a_{*}+0.02(\Sigma/\deg)$ for different values of $\iota$ across our model dataset. We also indicate the corresponding standard deviations.

We see that decreasing the value of $\iota$ from $90\degree$ greatly increases the spread from predicted fits, making the direct inference of $\chi$ and $a_{*}$ from $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ unreliable already for $\iota=60\degree$ (at $\iota=60\degree$ , the standard deviations are $\sigma\sim 58\degree$ for $\Delta-4\chi$ , and $\sigma\sim 0.97$ for $a_{*}+0.02\Sigma$ ). For $\iota$ of $45\degree$ or below, the distributions become clearly non-Gaussian, and take on new sub-structure as the underlying $\iota=90\degree$ assumption becomes undescriptive and the grid sampling peaks once again project out from the origin. This substructure suggests that, while being weak estimators on their own, $\Delta$ and $\Sigma$ might provide stronger constraints on $\chi$ and $a_{*}$ when used in combination with other observables, even in cases where the magnetic field is not aligned with the surface of the cone.

## Abstract

The Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) Collaboration produced the first image of the apparent shadow of the central black hole of Sagittarius A∗ (Sgr A∗). Sgr A∗ source structure varies significantly on timescales shorter than the duration of an observation, preventing improved data coverage through Earth rotation aperture synthesis. This rapid variability provides the opportunity to quantify intrinsic variability and separate time-variable emission features from stable signatures of strong gravity and the accretion environment. To infer the properties Sgr A∗ and its surrounding accretion flow, we perform Bayesian inference on a series of EHT data segments (“snapshots”). We directly fit parameters of a semi-analytic emission model jointly with complex station gains to snapshot visibilities, then extract estimates of the time-averaged, persistent source structure and temporal variability by stacking snapshots in a Bayesian hierarchical model. This approach successfully reproduces parameters of General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics simulations using synthetic EHT observations. Even with physically motivated assumptions about the Sgr A∗ environment, black hole spin and magnetic field parameters are poorly constrained by 2017 EHT observations. Our inference constrains other parameters, favoring a nearly face-on observer inclination ( $\theta_{\rm o}=9.2\degree\pm 3.6\degree\pm_{\rm v}11.6\degree$ ), an emission peak near the horizon ( $R_{\rm peak}=4.9\pm 0.1\pm_{\rm v}0.5\,GM/c^{2}$ ), near-vertical projected spin position angle ( $p.a.=7.3\degree\pm 7.08\degree\pm_{\rm v}43.5\degree$ counterclockwise from vertical), and dominant emission $43.4\degree\pm 2.0\degree\pm_{\rm v}5.9\degree$ above the equatorial plane, where we separate average structure uncertainty ( $\pm$ ) from the impacts of temporal variability and model misspecification ( $\pm_{\rm v}$ ).

## I Introduction

In 2017, the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) used an 8-element Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) array operating at $\lambda=1.3$ mm to observe Sagittarius A∗ (Sgr A∗), the radio source associated with the Supermassive Black Hole (SMBH) at the center of the Milky Way [1]. Image reconstructions displayed a bright ring of emission around a central brightness depression, or apparent “shadow”—features consistent with expectations for plasma accretion flows in a Kerr spacetime [19, 20, 21, 23, 24, 22, 17, 18, hereafter Sgr A* I-VIII].

In particular, this image morphology with a distinct “shadow” is a general prediction of models of optically thin plasmas around SMBHs as viewed by a distant observer [2, 43, 13, 30, 8, 49, e.g.]. In previous EHT studies, analysis in the visibility domain characterized morphological parameters of the likely ring-like image (e.g. diameter, orientation, thickness); in these analyses, the ring width was well constrained but the amplitude and orientation of ring asymmetry were poorly constrained and dependent on measurement methods [23]. Comparison with General Relativistic Magnetohydrodynamics (GRMHD) simulations led to strong constraints on Sgr A∗ magnetization but weak constraints on black hole spin [24]. Beyond these broad conclusions, the physical conditions of the accretion flow and near-horizon spacetime structure of the Sgr A∗ emitting region are largely unconstrained.

Sgr A∗ ( $M\approx 4\times 10^{6}M_{\odot}$ ) has a typical gravitational timescale $GM/c^{3}\approx 20$ s and time variability on the order of minutes to hours [15, 37, 36, see also 25, 23]. Traditional VLBI imaging relies on Earth-rotation aperture synthesis to increase sampling of the ( $u,v$ ) plane: as Earth rotates, baselines change their orientation with respect to the source, enabling greater Fourier coverage [62]. When source structure evolves on shorter timescales than a several-hour EHT observation, this technique cannot be employed to increase sampling of the ( $u,v$ ) plane and accurately reproduce the observed data. For Sgr A∗, the EHT found the magnitude of variability to be a substantial fraction of the correlated flux density in some cases [23]. This rapid intraday variability complicates attempts to infer physical parameters: visibility data is sparse and time variability must be handled in an informed manner. One approach to this problem—“snapshot modeling”—involves fitting parameters of interest over short snapshot observations of a source structure which is expected to be static.

Snapshot modeling of Sgr A∗ using the EHT observations was previously performed using a series of simple geometric models, finding that models with a ring-like structure best fit the emission from Sgr A∗ [23]. The ring diameter was well constrained, but other morphological parameters—like brightness asymmetries—were measured with less confidence [23]. Beyond inferring morphological parameters of on-sky emission, directly probing parameters of the physical accretion environment is of great interest for further understanding of the source. In this paper, we employ a lightweight, robust, phenomenological dual-cone emission model which provides a suitable and quick approximation to images generated from GRMHD simulations [11]. We use parallel tempered Markov Chain Monte Carlo (PTMCMC) sampling to fit the dual-cone model to visibility data, exploring the posteriors of physics-based model parameters. We then stack the snapshot posteriors in a Bayesian hierarchical model to form a global posterior. Figure 1 depicts the snapshot modeling scheme, whereby inference on individual snapshot visibilities produces parameter posteriors that inform a global hierarchical model.

In Section II, we discuss the semi-analytic emission model and its purpose in greater detail. Observations are briefly discussed in Section III. In Section IV, we consider methods of fitting EHT observations of Sgr A∗ and stacking posteriors across snapshots. In Section V, we outline results for a single snapshot, then the hierarchical model formed from all snapshots, and finally inference on synthetic data where the ground truths of several parameters are known. In Section VI, we consider the limitations of this analysis and the scientific implications of the results. Finally, we summarize our results in Section VII.

*Figure 1: Schematic depiction of the snapshot modeling methodology. We perform inference on complex visibilities from individual snapshots of varying coverage, jointly inferring physical model parameters and complex station gains. The resulting posteriors are then stacked in a global Bayesian hierarchical model, giving estimates for the average source structure and variable features. Top row, left to right: example ( $u,v$ )-coverage for individual snapshots, with snapshots ranging between poor coverage (a minimum of four baselines), such as the snapshot indexed as scan 27 (April 7, 2017 at 06:03); medium coverage, such as scan 114 (April 7, 2017 at 11:23); and good coverage (a maximum of 9 baselines), such as scan 157 (April 7, 2017 at 13:49 UTC). Even for the best-sampled snapshots, coverage is very sparse. Data taken at $227.07$ GHz are shown in blue and baselines of 3 G $\lambda$ and 6 G $\lambda$ are shown in green and red, respectively. Middle row, left to right: images drawn from the inferred posterior distributions corresponding to snapshot visibility data (scan 27, scan 114, and scan 157, respectively). Due to the sparsity of data in a single snapshot, many parameters are unconstrained and myriad different image morphologies fit the data. These morphologies contribute to structures in the mean and standard deviation images. Bottom row, left to right: mean and standard deviation (uncertainty) images from the global posterior, a Bayesian hierarchical model stacking the posteriors from every snapshot, with an average source structure distribution and a variability distribution. The mean image from the average source structure distribution indicates persistent morphological features across snapshots. The mean variability map shows the image features most subject to intra-snapshot variability.*

## II Semi-Analytic Accretion & Emission Model

GRMHD simulations are essential for interpreting observations of Low-Luminosity Active Galactic Nuclei (LLAGN), including the EHT observations of Sgr A∗ and M87∗. Beyond GRMHD simulations, there is a rich history of simulations exploring synchrotron-emitting plasma flows and accretion near the galactic center [65, 6, 14, 7, 56, 46, 24, 32, 10]. The computational demands of GRMHD simulations make them unsuitable for directly fitting observational data, whereby sophisticated sampling is performed in complicated, high-dimensional posteriors. This difficulty motivates an ongoing effort to develop lightweight semi-analytic emission models [8, 50, 55, some examples include] or neural surrogate models for GRMHD [31, 51] that can be used to describe and infer properties from these systems. Semi-analytic fits for Sgr A∗ have been previously performed using proto-EHT observations [8, see, e.g.], but these did not account for intraday source variability.

In this paper, we use the dual-cone emission model in Chang et al. 11, which expands on a similar equatorial plane emission model in Palumbo et al. 52. The dual-cone model considers synchrotron-emitting, magnetized plasma constrained to flow within two thin, oppositely oriented cones aligned with the black hole’s spin axis. The model is inherently axisymmetric. The cones open at an angle $\theta_{\rm s}$ from the spin axis. Emission is ray-traced in a Kerr geometry to a distant observer at inclination angle $\theta_{\rm o}$ from the spin axis. Several black hole, magnetic field configuration, and fluid configuration parameters inform the model. The model sufficiently reproduces images generated from a wide variety of GRMHD simulations while remaining efficient enough for Bayesian inference of model parameters on visibility data [11]. We therefore perform a kind of photogrammetry—reconstructing the three-dimensional physical structure and environmental conditions of Sgr A∗ from EHT data.

The spacetime structure in the model is calculated using the Kerr metric for a black hole of dimensionless spin $a_{\rm*}$ . The mass-to-distance ratio, $\theta_{\rm g}$ specifies a stretch modification on the image. A projected position angle $p.a.$ relative to the spin axis can be specified. Spin position angle $p.a.$ is measured East of North, or counterclockwise of vertical. As discussed, $\theta_{\rm o}$ specifies the inclination angle of a distant observer relative to the black hole spin axis and $\theta_{\rm s}$ specifies the opening angle of the cones relative to the spin axis. Unlike some previous EHT prescriptions, where positive spin indicates prograde fluid flow and negative spin retrograde, the sign of the spin in this model indicates whether it is aligned or anti-aligned with the observer’s line of sight.

The plasma flow is specified by the fluid speed in a Zero Angular Momentum Observer (ZAMO) frame, $\beta_{\rm v}$ , and the fluid velocity azimuthal angle in the ZAMO frame, $\chi$ . Magnetic field lines of the magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ thread the emission model. The magnetic field configuration is specified with $\iota$ , the angle of field lines with respect to the orthogonal of emission planes in the fluid frame, and $\eta$ , the azimuthal-tangential angle in the fluid frame. We prescribe a power law synchrotron emissivity profile with $R_{\rm peak}$ , the characteristic radius of emission, and $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ , the inner and outer exponents of the emissivity profile. The spectral index of emission is $\sigma$ . Emission is parallel transported along null geodesics to the distant observer. For this analysis, we use the resulting Stokes I intensity images containing both the $n=0$ (direct emission) and $n=1$ (a component of the indirect emission comprising the photon ring; see Johnson et al. 41) sub images, though other Stokes parameter maps incorporating polarization may also be produced from the model. Images produced with the dual-cone model typically feature a distinct brightness depression, or “shadow,” diffuse direct emission, and a thin, bright photon ring structure [41, 34, 33, for more discussion of the black hole photon ring, see, e.g.].

Though General Relativity predicts a direct relationship between the spin and mass-to-distance ratio—the angular gravitational radius, $\theta_{g}\equiv GM/(c^{2}D)$ —of a black hole and its asymptotic shadow diameter and shape [2], there are numerous degeneracies between black hole parameters and those of the emitting plasma for the direct emission [28, 27, 33, see, e.g.]. When attempting to constrain black hole parameters, it is therefore advantageous to perform Bayesian inference over a large parameter space and model the black hole and its emission parameters simultaneously. By exploring posteriors for many parameters, we may accurately characterize parameter values and uncertainties and better understand where degeneracies arise.

The semi-analytic model is ultimately an approximation of the physical environment around an SMBH and, therefore, has several key limitations. Conical emission surfaces are infinitely thin, and no optical depth prescription or full radiative transfer scheme is employed. While this enables fast image production and Bayesian inference on VLBI data, it limits the applicability of the model to relatively optically thin sources at mm wavelengths, misspecifying potentially optically thick sources. Time-variable structures/turbulence and asymmetries are not modeled. The model captures time-averaged structures and axisymmetric flows and is less flexible for analysis of time-variable structures in individual snapshots. The model uses several other simplifying assumptions: the emission region is compact; there is no radial evolution of the plasma velocity in the ZAMO frame, $\beta_{\rm v}$ ; and, as previously described, the emissivity model is a simplified, radially dependent double power law defined by $R_{\rm peak}$ , $p_{1}$ , and $p_{2}$ [11]. Snapshot inference on GRMHD simulations and Sgr A∗ data are subject to biases and systematic errors due to the lack of structural turbulence in the model [11]. Real data also include degrees of freedom not present in the dual-cone model. Nonetheless, the model’s ability to capture time-averaged GRMHD source structure motivates its use in this analysis. For further discussion about the dual-cone emission model, see Chang et al. 11 and Appendix A.

### II.1 Image Degeneracies

There are degeneracies in most image features—certain alterations could arise from a combination of a variety of physical parameters. For instance, the mass-to-distance ratio, characteristic emission radius, and cone opening angle can all resize the resulting image (the cone opening angle has a greater effect on the direct emission and shadow). The spin, fluid and magnetic field parameters ( $\chi$ , $p_{1}$ , $p_{2}$ , $\iota$ , $\beta_{\rm v}$ ), and the inclination strongly impact image morphology and brightness asymmetries. For further discussion of the semi-analytic emission model and the impacts of parameters on resulting images, see Appendix A. In this analysis, we fix the mass-to-distance ratio, eliminating, for instance, the degeneracy between mass-to-distance ratio and characteristic emission radius. However, other degeneracies remain, leading to complicated, multimodal posteriors in several variables—especially with sparse data in each snapshot. It is therefore important to accurately and thoroughly explore the posteriors of each parameter so we characterize all modes of interest.

## III Observations and Data Products

### III.1 VLBI Data Products

VLBI observations do not directly sample sky brightness distributions. Instead, at a time $t$ , they sample the complex visibilities of a source image $I(\bm{x},t)$ —the Fourier transform of the image—as originally described by the van Cittert-Zernike theorem:

$$ \tilde{I}(\bm{u},t)=\iint e^{2\pi i\bm{u}\cdot\bm{x}}I(\bm{x},t)\differential[2]{\boldsymbol{x}}. $$

Here, $\bm{x}=(x,y)$ are angular coordinates on the sky image and $\bm{u}=(u,v)$ are coordinates projected along baselines in units of the observing wavelength [62]. For a given baseline with coordinate $\bm{u}_{ab}$ , we denote the ideal visibility by $\tilde{I}_{ab}$ .

However, the observed visibilities $\hat{V}_{ab}$ are affected by factors introducing statistical and systematic errors, such as refraction and disturbances in the local atmosphere, instrumental bias, and cable length delay at individual telescope sites. We model these alterations in observed amplitude and phase as complex station gains $g$ at each specific telescope ( $g_{a}$ and $g_{b}$ here) for each timestamp. The observed visibility $\hat{V}_{ab}$ correlated on a baseline between stations $a$ and $b$ is given by

$$ \hat{V}_{ab}=g_{a}g_{b}^{*}\tilde{I}_{ab}+\epsilon_{ab}=\mathcal{V}_{ab}+\epsilon_{ab}, $$

where $\mathcal{V}_{ab}=g_{a}g_{b}^{*}\tilde{I}_{ab}$ is the model corrupted visibility and $\epsilon_{ab}$ is the statistical error on the baseline. We assume that $\epsilon_{ab}$ is a zero-mean, circularly symmetric, complex Gaussian random variable:

$$ \epsilon_{ab}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{ab}^{2})+i\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{ab}^{2}), $$

where $\sigma_{ab}$ is the statistical uncertainty for the baseline $ab$ .

### III.2 EHT Observations of Sgr A∗

For this analysis, we used EHT observations of Sgr A∗ taken on April 7, 2017—the day with the greatest $(u,v)$ -coverage in the 2017 observational campaign [21]. The data were preprocessed in a manner similar to the preprocessing pipeline in 21 and lightcurve normalized using the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA) Sgr A∗ lightcurve data [23]. In addition, to account for residual calibration uncertainties, refractive scattering in the interstellar medium, phase variations across the measurement frequency band, and leakage between right- and left-circularly polarized data, we inflate the statistical error budget $\sigma_{sb}$ for a baseline $J$ in snapshot $s$ :

$$ \sigma^{2}_{sJ}=\sigma_{{\rm th},sJ}^{2}+f^{2}|\hat{V}|^{2}_{sJ}+\sigma^{2}_{{\rm ref},sJ}, $$

where $\sigma_{{\rm th},sJ}$ is the thermal noise associated with a particular baseline and snapshot, the second term is multiplicative in the observed visibility amplitude (in order to capture residual, non-gain calibration errors, such as the aforementioned polarization leakage), and the third term is a refractive scattering noise model J18model1 described in 21. Following 20, we fix $f=0.02$ . To mitigate diffractive scattering, the data is deblurred as in Johnson et al. 42.

We then split the data into 120 s “snapshots,” flagging and removing those with fewer than four unique stations. The visibilities in each snapshot were coherently averaged over the 120 s window. For additional information on data processing for the snapshot fitting procedure, see 26, 20, 21, and 23. Each snapshot contains sparse complex visibility data. Snapshots vary by ( $u,v$ )-coverage and the number of baselines contributing to the snapshot observation. The top row of Figure 1 shows examples of ( $u,v$ )-coverage for individual snapshots.

## IV Bayesian Inference in the Visibility Domain: Snapshot Fitting

We use the Bayesian VLBI modeling package Comrade.jl outlined in Tiede 63 to form posteriors from visibility data in each snapshot. In particular, we specify a dual-cone sky emission model with the physical variables described in Section II as free parameters. We use complex visibilities instead of closure quantities to make full use of the sparse data. We therefore use an instrument model where gain amplitudes (with a Gaussian prior) and phases (with a von Mises prior) for each station present in a given snapshot are fit as free parameters.

Priors are specified in Table 1 for each physical parameter of interest. Since parameters of Sgr A∗ are largely unconstrained, we use wide priors in most variables. The observer’s inclination relative to the spin axis is essentially unconstrained (i.e., the observer inclination is given a flat prior $\theta_{o}\in[1\degree,89\degree]$ , and the spin can be positive or negative). The cone opening angle is constrained to values between $40\degree$ and $90\degree$ , informed by GRMHD simulations of the accretion environment of Sgr A∗ [11]. Notably, we fix the mass-to-distance ratio to $5.03\mu$ as with a delta distribution. Unlike M87∗, the value is well constrained for Sgr A∗ [37, 36, 15]. By fixing the mass-to-distance ratio, we remove some degeneracies and aid in the constraint of other parameters.

### IV.1 Forming Posteriors

For $N_{s}$ snapshots denoted by snapshot index $s$ —which we approximate as independent—we fit the dual-cone model to complex visibilities, determining posterior distributions for each parameter. In particular, we fit a parameter vector $\bm{\theta}_{s}$ . There are 13 physical parameters for the dual-cone emission model, which we denote with the parameter vector $\bm{\phi}_{s}$ . Since we fit complex visibilities, we also include an instrument model with parameter vector $\bm{S}_{s}$ . We define a single station gain model with a log-gain amplitude and gain phase: $g_{a}\equiv e^{\gamma_{a}+i\varphi_{a}}$ . The log-gain amplitude is specified using a normal distribution and the gain phase with a von Mises distribution. Gain phase is calibrated relative to a reference station. In $\bm{S}_{s}$ , there are two free parameters per station $I$ present in the data: $\bm{S}_{s}=\{\bm{\gamma}_{I,s},\bm{\varphi}_{I,s}\}$ . We jointly infer the physical parameters and instrument model $\bm{\theta}_{s}=\{\bm{\phi}_{s},\bm{S}_{s}\}$ .

In a single snapshot, the joint physical parameter and instrument model posterior is given by Bayes’ Theorem:

$$ P_{s}(\bm{\theta}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})=\frac{\mathcal{L}_{s}(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\theta}_{s})\pi_{s}(\bm{\theta}_{s})}{\mathcal{Z}_{s}(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})}, $$

where $\mathcal{L}_{s}$ denotes the likelihood, $\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}$ is the data available in snapshot $s$ , $\pi_{s}$ is the prior distribution as specified in Table 1, and $\mathcal{Z_{s}}$ is the Bayesian evidence or marginal likelihood. Following Equation 2 and Equation 3 the complex visibility likelihood is given by

$$ \mathcal{L}_{s}(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\theta}_{s})=\prod_{J}(2\pi\sigma^{2}_{s,J})^{-1}\exp[\frac{-|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s,J}-\mathcal{V}_{s,J}|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}_{s,J}}], $$

where $J$ is a multi-index that denotes a particular observation, time, and baseline.

A variety of degeneracies, or symmetries in the likelihood, are introduced by jointly fitting physical parameters and an instrument model, leading to non-identifiability or unconstrained degrees of freedom in the problem. We outline several prevalent examples here.

Rescaling the flux of the image, i.e., $\tilde{I}_{J}\rightarrow f\tilde{I}_{J}$ , can be absorbed by rescaling all gains: $g_{a}\to g_{a}/\sqrt{f}$ . There is therefore no constraint on the total flux of sources observed with VLBI. In our analysis, we normalize the model flux to $1.0$ and renormalize the observed visibilities by the ALMA lightcurve, so that the observed visibilities on short baselines (i.e., ALMA-APEX, SMA-JCMT) are unity up to residual thermal noise effects.

A global gain phase offset $\varphi_{I}\rightarrow\varphi_{I}+\phi_{0}$ has no effect on the likelihood, as the offset is canceled by its conjugate. Since likelihood is invariant under a global gain phase offset, we cannot measure the absolute phase. We infer gain phases relative to a specified reference station in each snapshot, which is selected alphabetically by station codes.

An image shift, $\tilde{I}(u,v)\to e^{2\pi i(u\Delta x+v\Delta y)}\tilde{I}(u,v)$ , is a phase gradient that, similarly to gain amplitudes, can be absorbed by a global redefinition of gain phases across all stations. In VLBI, this means that the likelihood is invariant to image shifts. However, the dual-cone model sets the image origin in Bardeen coordinates to reside with the black hole, removing this degeneracy [12].

### IV.2 Sampling Posteriors: Parallel Tempering

We explore parameter posteriors using a sampling algorithm called parallel tempering (PT) implemented in Pigeons.jl [59]. For a single snapshot, we run 20 tempering levels (separate chains) in parallel using MPI, with 24 threads in each tempering level task for ray-tracing the dual-cone emission model. The number of tempering levels was selected as $2\Lambda$ , where $\Lambda$ is the problem’s global communication barrier—around 10 for most snapshots. We perform 14 rounds of sampling, at which point the number of restarts is sufficient (greater than 100), the Bayesian evidence is stabilized, and the minimum and average swap acceptance rates $\alpha$ over the PT chains have stabilized and approached nearly the same value. We can be confident, therefore, that the sampling is robust, stable, and accurately characterizes the posterior distributions of all parameters.

During our analysis, we found that other sampling methods, such as Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (HMCMC) Sampling, Nested Sampling, and Dynamic Nested Sampling struggled to accurately capture the complicated, occasionally multimodal, and high-dimensional posterior in this problem. In particular, MCMC algorithms like Metropolis-Hastings and Gibbs sampling explore probability space by iteratively proposing and rejecting samples based on a target distribution. The chain may therefore struggle to traverse the low-probability regions between peaks.

The PT class of MCMC methods is capable of exploring complicated, multimodal distributions without getting stuck in a particular mode. If we are exploring a target distribution $\pi$ —in this case, the posterior distribution for a Bayesian inference problem—a series of distributions of increasing complexity and sampling difficulty (an annealing path) $\pi_{1},\pi_{2},...,\pi_{N}$ are constructed, with $\pi_{N}$ equal to the target $\pi$ . In an exploration phase, samples are obtained from each distribution in parallel. In the following communication phase, sample swaps between adjacent distributions are proposed, accepted or rejected with a Metropolis mechanism, and carried out with low communication cost [61]. This procedure enables the discovery of new regions in the target distribution. Pigeons.jl implements parallel tempering with distributed computation and strong parallelism invariance; output for a seed is identical regardless of the computational configuration, such as the number of threads, making it suitable for obtaining stable and robust scientific results [59]. For further information about the parallel tempering process used in this analysis, see Syed et al. 61, Surjanovic et al. 60, Surjanovic et al. 59, and Biron-Lattes et al. 3.

### IV.3 Hierarchical Stacking

After forming parameter posterior distributions $\bm{\theta}_{s}$ for all snapshots, we seek to extract the average posterior distributions to understand the persistent, stationary source structure. We build a Bayesian global/hierarchical model $\bm{\lambda}\equiv\langle\bm{\theta}_{s}\rangle_{T}$ , where the $T$ indicates that we average over all timestamps. The definition of the hierarchical model implies that each of the snapshot models $\bm{\theta}_{s}$ can be drawn from the global distribution $\bm{\lambda}$ . We are only interested in the effects of gains on the parameter inference of the physical model and not their actual average value. Thus, In forming the hierarchical model, we use the distribution $P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})=\int P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{s},\bm{S}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})\differential{\boldsymbol{S}_s}$ , where we have marginalized over the instrument model.

We define the global posterior $P_{s}(\bm{\lambda}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})$ from the snapshot posteriors $P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})$ by,

$$ P(\bm{\lambda}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})=\int P(\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})\differential{\boldsymbol{\phi}_s}, $$

where the integrand is the total posterior, which is unknown. Using Bayes’ rule, we rewrite the total posterior, up to a normalization constant:

$$ P(\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})\propto P(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s})P(\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s}). $$

We drop $\bm{\lambda}$ in $P(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s})$ by assuming the individual snapshots do not depend on $\bm{\lambda}$ directly. Expanding the second factor:

$$ P(\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})\propto P(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\phi}_{s})P(\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\lambda})P(\bm{\lambda}). $$

We then make the reasonable approximation that each $\bm{\theta}_{s}$ is independent conditioned on $\bm{\lambda}$ , though this is not precisely true: there is temporal correlation in reality. This allows us to decompose $P(\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}|\bm{\phi}_{s})$ by snapshot over all $T$ timestamps and manipulate:

$$ \displaystyle P(\bm{\lambda},\bm{\phi}_{s}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s}) \displaystyle\simeq P(\bm{\lambda})\prod_{i=1}^{T}P(\bm{\hat{V}}_{i}|\bm{\phi}_{i})P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda}) \displaystyle=P(\bm{\lambda})\prod_{i=1}^{T}\frac{P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{i})}{P(\bm{\phi}_{i})}P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda}), $$

where we have already specified $P(\bm{\phi}_{i})$ with the priors, $\pi_{s}$ , and the distributions $P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{i})$ are known through sampling on each snapshot. There is some freedom in specifying $P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})$ as a modeling choice. Since we want an idea for both the average global distribution and the spread to understand variability, we parameterize persistent and variable source structure by assuming truncated unit normal/Gaussian distributions (or von Mises for cyclic parameters) in mean and standard deviation with independent parameters $p$ : $P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})\sim\mathcal{TN}(\bm{\phi}_{p}|\bm{\mu}_{p},\bm{\sigma}_{p})$ . Thus $\bm{\mu_{p}}$ will indicate the average source structure values and $\bm{\sigma_{p}}$ will characterize parameter variability across snapshots.

Substituting the total posterior Equation 10 into Equation 7:

$$ P(\bm{\lambda}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})=P(\bm{\lambda})\prod_{i=1}^{T}\left(\int\frac{P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{i})}{P(\bm{\phi}_{i})}P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})\differential{\boldsymbol{\phi}_i}\right). $$

The integral is implicitly approximated with our sampling of the posterior $P(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{i})$ . With $N$ samples:

$$ P(\bm{\lambda}|\bm{\hat{V}}_{s})=P(\bm{\lambda})\prod_{i=1}^{T}\frac{1}{N}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{P_{s}(\bm{\phi}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})}{P(\bm{\phi}_{i})}\differential{\boldsymbol{\phi}_i}\right) $$

Finally, we perform parallel tempered MCMC sampling of the global average mean posterior and variability posterior. Each sample drawn from the global posterior is a Gaussian (or von Mises) distribution.

It is important to note that our stacking approximation overspecifies the priors for the hierarchical model. The overspecification is evident from considering Bayes’ rule,

$$ P(\bm{\theta}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})P(\bm{\lambda})=P(\bm{\lambda}|\bm{\theta}_{i})P(\bm{\theta}_{i}), $$

where we have specified $P(\bm{\theta}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})$ with a normal distribution $\mathcal{N}$ and $P(\bm{\mu})$ with a uniform distribution $\mathcal{U}(\mu_{l},\mu_{h})$ . From these considerations, we can analytically solve for $P(\bm{\theta}_{i})$ directly:

$$ P(\bm{\theta}_{i})=\int P(\bm{\theta}_{i}|\bm{\lambda})P(\bm{\lambda})d\bm{\lambda} $$

However, we have selected a uniform prior for each snapshot $P(\bm{\theta}_{i})=\mathcal{U}(l,h)$ , overspecifying the model. This procedure is nonetheless suitable for our purposes.

## V Results

### V.1 Posteriors from a Single Snapshot

To demonstrate snapshot fitting, we include the results of fitting one snapshot of Sgr A∗ data, indexed as scan 157 (April 7, 2017 at 13:49 UTC). Figure 8 shows the mean and standard deviation images produced by a series of images drawn from the sampled parameter posteriors, alongside a subset of those varied sample images. The mean image displays expected features of optically-thin plasma accretion flow in a Kerr metric, such as an inner shadow, diffuse direct ( $n=0$ ) emission, and a bright photon ring, with different brightness asymmetries in the $n=0$ and $n=1$ sub images. The data in a single snapshot is limited, resulting in unconstrained parameters and multimodality; there is therefore wide variation among images which properly fit the data, as shown in the standard deviation image. Because it aggregates a variety of image morphologies, the mean image is not indicative of the real physical sky brightness distribution.

The full corner plot showing the joint marginal probability densities for all pairs of physical parameters is shown in Figure 9 (aside from the mass-to-distance ratio, which is fixed). While several parameters are relatively well constrained, others, especially the spin, are unconstrained. In this snapshot, a low position angle and close to face-on observer inclination are preferred. The position angle is multimodal, with a wrap-around at $2\pi$ and another mode at $\pi$ . This snapshot favors a cone opening angle close to $40\degree$ rather than an opening angle closer to equatorial. The characteristic emission radius is well constrained due to the fixed mass-to-distance ratio eliminating degeneracies. Most parameters have support across the entire range. The results from this snapshot draw on sparse data and are subject to the temporal variability of Sgr A∗: results for a single snapshot likely do not capture persistent source structure.
